ad: CASE OF ŞERAFETTİN CAN ATALAY v. TÜRKİYE
sonuc: Violation of Article 5 - Right to liberty and security (Article 5-1 - Deprivation of liberty;Lawful arrest or detention;Procedure prescribed by law;Article 5-1-a - After conviction);Violation of Article 5 - Right to liberty and security (Article 5-4 - Review of lawfulness of detention);Violation of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 - Right to free elections - {general} (Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 - Free expression of the opinion of the people;Stand for election);Violation of Article 18 - Limitation on use of restrictions on rights (Article 18 - Restrictions for unauthorised purposes);Respondent State to take individual measures (Article 46-2 - Individual measures);Respondent State to take measures of a general character (Article 46-2 - General measures);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
paragraflar: CASE OF ŞERAFETTİN CAN ATALAY v. TÜRKİYE
(Application no. 11503/24)

Art 5 § 1 • Deprivation of liberty • Art 5 § 1 (a) • Continued detention of a lawyer and human-rights defender after his election as a Member of Parliament and the Court of Cassation’s refusal to release him despite Constitutional Court judgments in his favour finding a violation of his rights to liberty and security • Continued detention neither “lawful” nor “in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law”

Art 5 § 4 • Failure to provide the applicant with a review of the lawfulness of his detention resulting from the non-implementation of the Constitutional Court’s judgments • Court’s finding that an individual application before the Constitutional Court did not provide the applicant with a review within the meaning of Art 5 § 4 strictly limited to the specific circumstances of the present case

Art 3 P1 • Free expression of the opinion of the people • Stand for election • Applicant’s inability to take his seat in Parliament and the eventual termination of his parliamentary mandate on account of his conviction and unlawful detention amounting to an unjustified interference

Art 18 ( Art 5 and Art 3 P1) • Restrictions for unauthorised purposes • Applicant’s continued detention in the absence of recognition of his parliamentary immunity – resulting from the Court of Cassation’s refusal to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgments – pursued the ulterior purpose of silencing him and stifling pluralism • Continued detention liable to have a dissuasive effect on the work of human-rights defenders

Art 46 • Execution of judgment • Individual measures • Respondent State required to take all necessary measures to end the applicant’s detention and secure his immediate release, allowing him to take up his seat in the Parliament and perform his parliamentary functions • General measures • Respondent State required to take all measures to provide that Constitutional Court judgments are fully implemented and to prevent similar future violations
Prepared by the Registry. Does not bind the Court.
This judgment will become final in the circumstances set out in Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.
In the case of Şerafettin Can Atalay v. Türkiye,
The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:
Arnfinn Bårdsen, President, Saadet Yüksel, Jovan Ilievski, Oddný Mjöll Arnardóttir, Gediminas Sagatys, Stéphane Pisani, Hugh Mercer, judges, and Dorothee von Arnim, Deputy Section Registrar,

the application (no. 11503/24) against the Republic of Türkiye lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national, Mr Şerafettin Can Atalay (“the applicant”), on 16 April 2024;
the decision by a Chamber of the Second Section to apply Rule 41 of the Rules of Court and to grant the applicant’s request for priority treatment of the application;
the decision to give notice of the application to the Turkish Government (“the Government”);
the parties’ observations;
Having deliberated in private on 29 September 2026,
Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

1. The case concerns the applicant’s continued detention following his election as a Member of Parliament (“MP”) in the general elections of 14 May 2023 and the Court of Cassation’s refusal to release him despite the Constitutional Court’s judgments in his favour, in which the latter court found violations of his right to liberty and security and his right to stand for election and to engage in political activity. The applicant relied on Articles 5 § 1, 5 § 4, 6, 7, 10, 11 and 18 of the Convention, as well as Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.
2. The applicant was born in 1976 and lives in Istanbul. He was represented by Mr F. İlkiz and Mr E. İşler, lawyers practising in Istanbul.
3. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Abdullah Aydın, Head of the Department of Human Rights of the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Türkiye.
4. The facts of the case may be summarised as follows.

5. The applicant is a lawyer and human-rights defender. During the widespread protest movements in 2013 referred to as “the Gezi Park events” (for more information, see Kavala (no. 2) v. Türkiye [GC], no. 2170/24, §§ 17-21, 25 August 2026, and Kavala v. Turkey, no. 28749/18, §§ 15-22, 10 December 2019), he was a member of the collective called “Taksim Solidarity” (Taksim Dayanışması) – a grouping of several associations, trade unions, professional organisations and political parties, set up to bring those bodies together and to coordinate and organise the protests.
criminal proceedings against the applicant and his election as mp
The prosecution of the applicant

6. On 19 February 2019 the Istanbul public prosecutor issued an indictment against the applicant and fifteen other persons who had taken part in the Gezi Park events, including actors, NGO leaders and journalists (for detailed information about the indictment of 19 February 2019, see Kavala (no. 2), cited above, §§ 23-25, and Kavala, cited above, §§ 47-56). The public prosecutor accused the persons concerned, in particular, of having attempted to overthrow the government by force and violence within the meaning of Article 312 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237 – see paragraph 56 below), and of having committed numerous breaches of public order, such as damaging public property, the desecration of places of worship and of cemeteries, the unlawful possession of dangerous substances, and looting. He concluded as follows:

“... before the Gezi insurrection, known as the “Gezi Park events”, all the defendants had been in training with the aim of overthrowing the government; they began to implement their plan in May 2013; legal and illegal groups, as well as illegal groups that were ostensibly legal and seemingly independent of each other, began to act by converging around a single aim; all the defendants sought to incite the public to take to the streets by organising so-called “non-violent” actions that were intended to gain public sympathy; they made numerous appeals and tried to increase participation in collective demonstrations by claiming that the police had intervened violently in the demonstrations; their aim was to plunge the country and society into chaos, as had occurred during the 1960 and 1980 coups d’état, by providing left-wing terrorist organisations with a favourable environment and attempting to overthrow the Government of the Republic of Turkey or to prevent it from exercising its functions; they very probably wished to force the Government to resign and to hold early elections, as in certain foreign countries; should this attempt fail, they intended to lay the groundwork for a civil war and a coup d’état, as in Syria and Egypt; the armed terrorist organisation FETÖ/PDY made similar attempts; after the Gezi insurrection had ended ... the armed terrorist organisation FETÖ/PDY became involved with the aim of achieving the same goal; in the light of the evidence in the case file, it has been found that the suspects committed the offences with which they are charged.”

7. In so far as his conclusions concerned the applicant, the public prosecutor relied on the applicant’s profile and his previous activities. In that regard, he found the applicant to be a spokesperson for the Taksim Solidarity collective (see paragraph 5 above) and affiliated with Mr Kavala, the applicant in Kavala and Kavala (no. 2) (both cited above), who was one of the other suspects on the indictment. Relying mainly on transcripts of telephone conversations, video footage of the Gezi Park events and social media posts, the public prosecutor referred to a number of actions carried out by the applicant. Those actions included the applicant’s telephone conversations with Mr Kavala and several other persons (which mainly related to organisational matters during the Gezi Park events such as arranging meetings); his presence at the Gezi Park events (in particular, the speeches he had made to the protesters) and other protests concerning the urbanisation of green areas; his social media posts, mainly on the developments in the administrative court proceedings regarding the cancellation of various urban plans; and a number of telephone conversations with various correspondents, including journalists, about those administrative proceedings.
The criminal proceedings in the Istanbul Assize Court and the Istanbul Regional Court of Appeal

8. On 25 April 2022 the Istanbul Assize Court found that the applicant was an important member of, and lawyer to, the Taksim Solidarity group, which had been inciting demonstrations through social media since 2012. On 27 May 2013 members of Taksim Solidarity had set up tents in Gezi Park and invited demonstrators to join them there. The ensuing protests had led to the occupation of the park and attacks on the security forces using sticks, stones and Molotov cocktails. As shown in a great deal of CCTV footage, the applicant had actively participated in the protest meetings; had shared provocative and misleading social media posts and press statements, encouraging the protesters to use violence against the security forces; and had made statements and chanted slogans during the protests by megaphone, leading to a riot. The Assize Court listed a number of telephone conversations and meetings between the applicant and some of the other accused, observing that he had been in contact with those individuals from 2011 onwards (see Kavala (no. 2), cited above, § 51, with regard to the Assize Court’s findings that the applicant had been in contact with Mr Kavala). It concluded that the applicant had engaged in activities relating to the incitement of an attempted uprising which had been planned to intensify and to expand throughout the entire country. During the course of the attempted uprising, the applicant had incited the demonstrators to action and had thus laid the groundwork for the escalation of the violence.

9. The Assize Court therefore convicted the applicant, together with seven of his co-defendants, of attempting to overthrow the government or to prevent it from performing its functions under Article 312 of the Criminal Code. It sentenced him to aggravated life imprisonment. Finding that the applicant had aided and abetted the commission of the offence by the main perpetrator, Mr Kavala, within the meaning of Article 39 of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 56 below), the court reduced his sentence to 18 years’ imprisonment. Lastly, the court made a separate order for the applicant’s detention. The trial court decided that there was no need to give a judgment on the numerous other offences the applicant had been charged with, finding that the actions that had led to those charges were within the definition of the force and violence that were constituent elements of the offence of attempting to overthrow the government or to prevent it from performing its functions.

10. On 28 December 2022 the Istanbul Regional Court of Appeal dismissed an appeal by the applicant, finding that the first-instance court had not erred in its assessment and findings. The Court of Appeal ordered the continued detention of the applicant and his co-defendants, given the severity of the sentences imposed and the fact that the charges were among those for which there was a statutory presumption of the existence of grounds for detention in the Code of Criminal Procedure (Law no. 5271). Finding that the evidence gave rise to a strong suspicion that the applicant and his co‑defendants had committed an offence, the Court of Appeal held that any other measure than detention would be insufficient.
11. On 16 January 2023 the applicant appealed to the Court of Cassation.
The applicant’s election as an MP and the proceedings in the Court of Cassation regarding his request to benefit from parliamentary immunity

12. While his appeal was still pending in the Court of Cassation, the applicant was elected as an MP for Hatay in the parliamentary elections of 14 May 2023, having stood for the Workers Party of Türkiye.

13. Subsequently, on 25 May 2023 the applicant applied to the Court of Cassation for his release and for the stay of the criminal proceedings against him under Article 83 of the Constitution, which deals with parliamentary immunity (see paragraph 53 below). He argued that he could not be detained and tried unless the Turkish Grand National Assembly (“the National Assembly”) had decided to lift his parliamentary immunity. According to him, while Article 83 § 2 referred to exceptions to parliamentary immunity listed in Article 14 of the Constitution, what those exceptions were could not be established in a clear and foreseeable manner. In that regard, he referred to previous judgments of the Constitutional Court (see paragraphs 60-61 below). He also pointed to a decision of the plenary criminal divisions of the Court of Cassation (“the plenary criminal divisions”) regarding the interpretation of Articles 83 and 14 of the Constitution and the binding nature of the judgments delivered by the Constitutional Court in respect of individual applications (see paragraph 62 below). Referring to the Constitutional Court’s findings in similar cases of a violation of the right to stand for election and to engage in political activity under Article 67 of the Constitution (see paragraph 54 below), the applicant also argued that his continued detention constituted a violation of that right.

14. On 13 July 2023 the Third Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation found that the applicant’s request for his release and the suspension of the criminal proceedings against him required it to examine his claim to parliamentary immunity. In view of the nature of the offence, that examination would be carried out with reference to Articles 83 and 14 of the Constitution (see paragraph 53 below). Article 83 § 2 of the Constitution provided two exceptions to parliamentary immunity: situations where an MP was caught in the course of committing an offence punishable by a heavy penalty (in flagrante delicto) and the cases falling within the scope of Article 14 of the Constitution, provided that an investigation had begun before the election. The legislature had not specified the offences that would fall within the scope of Article 14 but had deliberately left the determination of its scope to the courts. In that regard, although the Constitutional Court had found in previous individual review cases that Article 14 did not establish the exceptions to parliamentary immunity in a clear and foreseeable manner, that court could not render a Constitutional provision unenforceable through decisions taken within the scope of the individual application mechanism. That mechanism was subsidiary to the court’s main function, namely, a judicial review of legal provisions. Legal certainty came not only from legislation but also from case-law, provided that the law was accessible and foreseeable.

15. The Court of Cassation went on to analyse what offences would fall within the scope of Article 14 of the Constitution. In that regard, it cited the definition of terrorism in Article 1 of Law no. 3713 on the Prevention of Terrorism Act (“Law no. 3713”), and the principal terrorist offences in Article 3 of the same Act. These included, among other things, Articles 309 and 312 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237 – see paragraph 56 below), which govern the offence of violation of the Constitution and offences against the Government respectively. The Court of Cassation further referred to the explanatory memoranda of Articles 309 and 312 of the Criminal Code, which stated that the legal interest protected by these provisions was the principle of the constitutional order and that attempts directed against one of the fundamental bodies of the constitutional order would be punished to the same extent as if the full offence had been carried out. The Court of Cassation concluded that the offences in Article 3 of Law no. 3713, including Article 312 of the Criminal Code, fell within the scope of Article 14 of the Constitution.
16. With respect to the applicant’s case, the Court of Cassation stated as follows:

“In the present case, which has not yet been decided on its merits, it appears from the findings of the first-instance court that – in the context of the events publicly known as the Gezi Park protests, which began as demonstrations against the Taksim Artillery Barracks Project that were planned as part of the Taksim Pedestrianisation Project and later spread nationwide and escalated into mass violent incidents, resulting in 746 unlawful meetings and demonstrations in 78 provinces, damage to 280 workplaces, 259 private vehicles, 103 police vehicles, one residence, one police station, five public buildings and twelve party buildings, as well as loss of life and numerous injuries – the accused Şerafettin Can Atalay engaged in activities aimed at initiating and intensifying an attempted uprising to be carried out according to a plan and to be spread throughout the country. It was found that he was an influential member of the Taksim Solidarity group and that his statements and calls had contributed to the escalation of the violence. It was also found that he had facilitated the offence by assisting [Mr Kavala], the principal perpetrator, before or during the commission of the offence. His actions were therefore regarded as constituting the offence of aiding an attempt to bring down the Government of the Republic of Türkiye or to prevent it from performing its function in whole or in part, and he was convicted and detained pursuant to Article 312(1) and Article 39 of Law no. 5237.

In view of the fact that the offence imputed to the accused – attempting, by use of force and violence, to bring down the Government of the Republic of Türkiye or to prevent it from performing its functions – falls within the scope of Article 14 of the Constitution, and that the investigation had begun before the election, it was concluded that, pursuant to the second sentence of paragraph 2 of Article 83 of the Constitution, he did not benefit from parliamentary immunity, and that the proceedings should therefore continue under the usual procedural rules.”
17. The Court of Cassation therefore unanimously rejected the applicant’s request for his release and for the suspension of the criminal proceedings against him (see paragraph 13 above).

18. On 14 July 2023 the applicant challenged that decision, arguing that the Court of Cassation did not have jurisdiction to interpret constitutional provisions and should implement the Constitutional Court’s binding judgments regarding the interpretation of the relevant provisions. There was no legislative clarification of the offences falling within the scope of Article 14 of the Constitution, which led the trial courts to interpret that Constitutional provision. That interpretation could not be considered clear and foreseeable. It would also render parliamentary immunity under Article 83 of the Constitution and the right to stand for election and to engage in political activity under Article 67 of the Constitution futile. The applicant further maintained that in deciding to detain him, the Istanbul Assize Court had failed to make an individualised assessment or to put forward any arguments regarding his risk of absconding.

19. On 17 July 2023, by four votes to one, the Fourth Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation rejected the applicant’s objection to the decision of 13 July 2023 (see paragraphs 14-17 above). The dissenting judge held that restrictions on the right to stand for election and to engage in political activity under Article 67 of the Constitution must remain an exception and any restrictions which were not legally certain would have to be interpreted narrowly. Article 14 of the Constitution did not refer to specific offences and any interpretation in that regard would breach the principle of legal certainty. Article 14 was neither clear nor foreseeable, which could also be observed from the discrepancy between the case-law of the Constitutional Court and that of the Court of Cassation. He therefore held that the applicant should benefit from parliamentary immunity and should be released.
The Court of Cassation’s decision on appeal

20. On 28 September 2023 the Court of Cassation upheld the Istanbul Assize Court’s judgment of 25 April 2022 (see paragraphs 8 and 9 above) in so far as it concerned the applicant and five of his co-defendants. The Court of Cassation repeated the narrative of events described in the indictment of 19 February 2019 (see paragraph 6 above) and concluded that the Gezi Park events had not been a spontaneous and unpredictable reaction by the public but an insurrection (kalkışma), the result of a social engineering project planned by various activists over the course of the previous two years. The Court of Cassation found that the entities that supported and directed the events had included the Foundation for an Open Society, which was a branch of the Open Society Institute led by an international speculator, G.S.; the Anadolu Kültür limited company, which had been established by Mr Kavala; and three groups, namely, Taksim Group, Taksim Solidarity and Coordinated Forums.

21. The Court of Cassation found that the applicant, who had set up Taksim Solidarity (see paragraph 5 above), had started an intensive campaign against the pedestrianisation of Taksim Square starting from 2012, had actively taken part in encouraging the Gezi Park events and had incited an uprising through his social media posts. He had had intensive contact with the other defendants prior to and during the events and had taken part in meetings of Coordinated Forums, in order to maintain the momentum of the events and to spread them around the country. The Court of Cassation again referred to the damage caused during the events and held that the applicant had provoked violence aimed at overthrowing the government.

22. The Court of Cassation concluded that the acts committed by the applicant had constituted the offence of attempting to overthrow the Government within the meaning of Article 312 of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 56 below), whereas he had been convicted by the Assize Court of aiding an attempt to overthrow the Government. Nevertheless, as no appeal had been lodged regarding the classification of the offence, it did not quash the judgment of the Assize Court on that ground and went on to uphold it.

23. As regards the applicant’s specific situation following his election as an MP, the Court of Cassation repeated the findings in its decision of 13 July 2023 (see paragraphs 14-17 above), concluding that the applicant did not benefit from parliamentary immunity.
the first individual application to the constitutional court following the applicant’s election as MP and subsequent proceedings
The first individual application

24. On 20 July 2023 – after the Court of Cassation’s rejection of his request for his release and for the suspension of the criminal proceedings because of his parliamentary immunity (see paragraphs 14-17 above), but before the decision of the Court of Cassation upholding the Assize Court’s judgment (see paragraphs 20-23 above) – the applicant lodged an individual application with the Constitutional Court, complaining about violations of his right to liberty and security, his right to a fair trial and his rights to vote, to be elected and to engage in political activity. He argued, inter alia, that his continued detention was unlawful and that he should benefit from parliamentary immunity in line with Article 83 of the Constitution (see paragraph 53 below). In rejecting his application, the Court of Cassation had failed to follow the Constitutional Court’s earlier decisions on the issue. Moreover, his detention as a result of his conviction was not in accordance with the law and no reasons for his detention had been provided.
25. On 28 September 2023 the Court of Cassation upheld the applicant’s conviction (see paragraphs 20-23 above).

26. On 25 October 2023 in Şerafettin Can Atalay (2) (B. No. 2023/53898) the Constitutional Court found, by nine votes to five, that there had been a violation of the applicant’s right to liberty and security and his right to stand for election and to engage in political activity under Articles 19 and 67 of the Constitution, respectively (see paragraph 54 below). It found that neither the interference with the applicant’s right to stand for election nor his continued detention were prescribed by law.

27. Reiterating its findings in previous cases lodged by other applicants (Ömer Gergerlioğlu, B. No. 2019/10634, 1 July 2021, and Leyla Güven, B. No. 2018/26689, 7/4/2022 – see paragraphs 60-61 below), the Constitutional Court stated that there were no clear and foreseeable constitutional or legal provisions from which the scope of Article 14 of the Constitution could be established. It stated that Articles 14 and 83 of the Constitution should be interpreted using a rights-based approach. However, not only had the domestic courts failed to take that approach but there existed no clear and foreseeable guidance requiring that to be done. Nor were there any substantive or procedural safeguards governing the application of the exception set out in those provisions. The Constitutional Court further emphasised the absence of legal safeguards which might otherwise prevent arbitrary or disproportionate interferences with the rights of elected parliamentarians. These included safeguards against politically motivated accusations or unnecessary restrictions impeding the exercise of parliamentary functions. Moreover, there was no legal basis for the finding of the Third Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation that the legislature had deliberately left the determination of the scope of Article 14 of the Constitution to be developed by the courts (see paragraph 14 above). This was also demonstrated by an inconsistency in the Court of Cassation’s case-law regarding the offences which fell within the scope of that provision.

28. The Constitutional Court stated that although in its judgment in Ömer Gergerlioğlu (see paragraph 60 above) it had pointed to the State authorities’ general regulatory obligations, in the present case the Court of Cassation had interpreted the scope of Article 14 so as to restrict the applicant’s constitutional rights, thereby breaching those rights and failing to implement the Constitutional Court’s decision. In finding a violation of the applicant’s rights under Article 67 of the Constitution, the Constitutional Court concluded that the interference with the applicant’s right to stand for election and to engage in political activity was not lawful because there had been no legal or constitutional framework making it legally certain or foreseeable. As regards his right to liberty and security under Article 19 of the Constitution (see paragraph 54 below), it reiterated its findings regarding Article 67 and held that even where the initial reason for detention was sentencing after conviction, when circumstances arose that undermined its lawfulness – such as a legal or constitutional obstacle preventing continued detention or a judicial decision requiring release – the connection between the conviction and the deprivation of liberty would no longer exist. In the present case, the question whether the applicant would benefit from parliamentary immunity under Article 83 of the Constitution was a factor directly affecting the lawfulness of his continued detention. Given that he should have benefited from parliamentary immunity, there was no legal basis for his continued detention.

29. The Constitutional Court transmitted its judgment to the Istanbul Assize Court, stating that it was required to give the applicant redress by suspending the execution of his sentence, ordering his release from prison, and reopening and staying the criminal proceedings against him.

30. The dissenting judges repeated the same submissions they had made in the two previous cases cited in the judgment (see paragraph 27 above). They considered that although the legislature had not specified the offences which fell within the scope of Article 14 of the Constitution, the courts were well placed to determine which offences were concerned.
The subsequent proceedings in the Assize Court and the Court of Cassation

31. On 1 November 2023 the Assize Court referred the case to the Court of Cassation, stating that the violations found by the Constitutional Court arose from the decision of the Court of Cassation. It also observed that while the individual application was pending in the Constitutional Court, the Court of Cassation had upheld the applicant’s conviction (see paragraphs 20-23 above), and that it would therefore have to deal with the case taking into account the new legal situation.

32. On 8 November 2023 the Third Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation reiterated the findings in its decision of 13 July 2023 (see paragraphs 14-17 above). It held that the legislature had intentionally omitted to list the offences to which Article 14 of the Constitution would apply, allowing the first-instance and appeal courts to make their own assessments of any offence committed by an MP. In that respect, the Court of Cassation concluded once again that the offence of which the applicant had been convicted fell within the scope of Article 14 of the Constitution. The Constitutional Court had disregarded the Court of Cassation’s decision of 28 September 2023 upholding the applicant’s conviction (see paragraphs 20‑23 above), which predated the Constitutional Court’s judgment of 25 October 2023 finding that the applicant’s rights had been violated (see paragraphs 26-29 above). The Constitutional Court had in effect acted as a fourth-instance court and had gone so far as to threaten the members of the Court of Cassation. It had therefore exceeded its jurisdiction and abused its authority.
33. In that regard, the Court of Cassation stated as follows:

“The Constitutional Court has not only interfered in the proper sphere of the legislature by rejecting specific legal provisions, but has also acted like a supervisory authority and a “super appeal court” over other appellate courts, despite the fact that there is no hierarchical relationship between itself and these courts under the Constitution.

The legislative, executive and judicial branches represent a distribution of functions. The position of the judiciary differs from that of the other two branches. When the judiciary adopts an activist approach, it tends to lose its legitimacy and become prone to a loss of public confidence. What is expected of the judiciary is that it should deliver decisions in accordance with the legal provisions, the Constitution and, above all, the principles of law.

By engaging in judicial activism, the Constitutional Court has, through decisions that are contrary to the Constitution – such as rendering constitutional provisions which it cannot formally review unenforceable, accepting individual applications without the exhaustion of all administrative and judicial remedies provided for by law, intervening in investigations and making prosecutions ineffective – considered its powers and functions to be superior to the Constitution and the law. In doing so, it has, in a sense, nullified the Constitution and so led to a loss of public confidence and to debates regarding its legitimacy.”

34. The Court of Cassation therefore decided unanimously not to implement the Constitutional Court’s decision, which it found to have no legal significance, and to transmit its own decision to the National Assembly so as to have it remove the applicant’s mandate as an MP. It also decided to make a criminal complaint against the members of the Constitutional Court who had voted for a finding of a violation of the applicant’s rights, for unlawfully exceeding the limits of their authority. There is no information in the Court’s case file regarding the outcome of that criminal complaint.

35. On 10 November 2023 the Court of Cassation issued a press statement, which it said was to address the public controversy surrounding the decisions of the two superior courts in the applicant’s case. It stated that it was the highest appellate authority in the judicial system and that the Constitution did not establish a hierarchy among superior courts. Given that the individual application mechanism constituted a subsidiary remedy, the Constitutional Court had no jurisdiction to rehear cases decided by the appellate courts. Nevertheless, the Constitutional Court had sometimes acted as a “super appeal court”, exceeded the constitutional limits, and turned appeal courts’ decisions down, thereby leading the legal system to chaos. In the applicant’s case, the Constitutional Court had disregarded the will of the legislature and the effect of Article 14 of the Constitution. The Constitutional Court’s finding that, by interpreting Article 14 of the Constitution in a restrictive manner, the Court of Cassation had violated the Constitution (see paragraph 28 above) was legally unacceptable.
the second individual application to the constitutional court and subsequent proceedings
The second individual application

36. On 24 November 2023 the applicant filed a further individual application with the Constitutional Court, making the same complaints as in his first individual application (see paragraph 24 above). This time, he also complained that the Assize Court and Court of Cassation had not implemented the Constitutional Court’s judgment in his favour.

37. On 21 December 2023 the Constitutional Court, by eleven votes to three, found violations of the applicant’s right to liberty and security and of his right to stand for election and to engage in political activity (Şerafettin Can Atalay (3), B. No. 2023/99744). It also found, unanimously, a violation of the applicant’s right to individual application under Article 148 § 3 of the Constitution (see paragraph 54 below). The Constitutional Court stated that the violations found had resulted from the failure to implement its previous judgment of 25 October 2023 (see paragraphs 26-29 above).

38. The Constitutional Court observed that on an individual application its powers and functions were not limited to assessing whether or not a constitutional right had been violated. It also had power to direct a remedy for the violation under section 50 § 1 of Law no. 6216 on the establishment and rules of procedure of the Constitutional Court (see paragraph 55 below). When the Constitutional Court found a violation and stated what measures should be taken to put an end to the violation and redress its effects, the courts concerned – which had no discretion in the matter – must commence the procedures required. Moreover, the judgment was binding on those courts under Article 153 of the Constitution (see paragraph 54 below), which did not provide for any exceptions. A failure to implement the Constitutional Court’s decisions regarding individual applications would undermine the individual and societal confidence in the rule of law and would cause harm to the constitutional order.

39. In that respect, the Constitutional Court referred to the Court’s decision in Uzun v. Turkey ((dec.), no. 10755/13, 30 April 2013); its judgment in Mehmet Hasan Altan v. Turkey (no. 13237/17, 20 March 2018); a previous decision it had delivered in the case of Kadri Enis Berberoğlu (3) (see paragraphs 57-58 below); and a decision of the plenary criminal divisions of the Court of Cassation dated 26 October 2022, in which the latter court had emphasised that it was for the Constitutional Court to interpret Article 14 of the Constitution and to determine its scope and that the Constitutional Court’s decisions were binding (see paragraph 62 below). The Constitutional Court also referred to several previous decisions of the Third Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation – which had decided not to implement its judgments in the applicant’s case – and a decision of a civil division of the Court of Cassation which had pointed out that Constitutional Court decisions were binding (see paragraphs 63-64 below).
Reiterating its previous order as to relief (see paragraph 29 above), the Constitutional Court referred its judgment to the Istanbul Assize Court.

40. The dissenting judges of the Constitutional Court maintained that that court’s jurisdiction was limited to assessing whether acts and omissions complied with the provisions of the Constitution and did not extend to the review of a constitutional provision. They argued that while there was no provision setting out the offences to which Article 14 of the Constitution applied, the scope of that provision could be determined by the case-law of the ordinary courts and the Court of Cassation. Consistent decisions of those courts had made it clear that the offence in Article 312 of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 56 below) fell within that scope. Article 14 of the Constitution was therefore not unforeseeable. The dissenting judges considered that if the Constitutional Court’s decisions were not implemented, the result would be a violation of the right to individual application under Article 148 of the Constitution and that it would not affect the right to liberty and security or the right to stand for election and to engage in political activity.
The subsequent proceedings in the Assize Court and the Court of Cassation
41. On 27 December 2023 the Assize Court decided to refer the case to the Court of Cassation for the same reasons as those given in its decision of 1 November 2023 (see paragraph 31 above).

42. On 3 January 2024 the Third Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation decided not to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgment, mainly for the reasons given in its previous decision of 8 November 2023 (see paragraphs 32-33 above). It observed that the present case was not the first in which the Court of Cassation had declined to implement a judgment of the Constitutional Court on an individual application and that the Constitutional Court had no power to interpret constitutional provisions in a manner that would deprive them of all meaning. It again transmitted its decision to the National Assembly.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICE
53. The provisions of the Constitution relevant to the applicant’s status as an MP and his legal immunity read as follows:
The prohibition of the abuse of fundamental rights and freedoms

“None of the rights and freedoms set out in the Constitution may be exercised in a manner intended to undermine the territorial integrity of the State and the unity of the nation or to extinguish the democratic and secular Republic founded on human rights.

None of the provisions of the Constitution may be interpreted in a manner that would enable the State or individuals to engage in activities intended to destroy the fundamental rights and freedoms embodied in the Constitution or to restrict them beyond the limits prescribed by the Constitution.
The penalties to be imposed on those who engage in activities that contravene these provisions shall be regulated by law.”

“Members of the Turkish Grand National Assembly shall not be liable for the votes they cast or statements they make in the course of the Assembly’s work or for the views they express in the Assembly, nor, unless the Assembly decides otherwise, at a session at which a proposal made by the Bureau is discussed, for repeating or disseminating such views outside the Assembly.

A member who is alleged to have committed an offence before or after being elected shall not be arrested, questioned, detained or tried unless the Assembly decides otherwise. This provision shall not apply where the member is caught in the course of committing an offence punishable by a heavy penalty, or, where an investigation was commenced before the member was elected, in cases under Article 14 of the Constitution. However, in such cases the appropriate authority shall notify the Turkish Grand National Assembly of the situation immediately and directly.

The implementation of a criminal sentence imposed on a member of the Turkish Grand National Assembly either before or after his or her election shall be suspended until he or she ceases to be a member; limitation does not run during a member’s term of office.
The investigation and prosecution of a re-elected member shall be subject to a fresh decision by the Assembly to lift immunity.
Political party groups in the Turkish Grand National Assembly shall not hold debates or take decisions regarding parliamentary immunity.”
Termination of parliamentary mandate

The termination of a parliamentary mandate in the event of a final conviction or restriction shall take place on notification of the final court decision in the case to the Plenary [of the National Assembly].
54. The other relevant provisions of the Constitution read as follows:
Personal liberty and security
“Everyone has the right to personal liberty and security.

No one may be deprived of his or her liberty except for the [following] situations, the forms and conditions [of which] are governed by law: where a penalty or security measure involving deprivation of liberty has been imposed by a court; ...

Everyone who is deprived of his or her liberty for any reason whatsoever shall be entitled to apply to an authorised judicial authority for a speedy decision on his or her case and for his or her immediate release if the detention is not lawful.
Rights to vote, to stand for election and to engage in political activity

“Citizens shall have the right to vote, to stand for election, to engage in political activities independently or as members of a political party and to take part in referendums, in accordance with the rules laid down by law.
The exercise of these rights shall be regulated by law.
Approval of international treaties

International agreements duly brought into domestic law have the force of law. No appeal to the Constitutional Court shall be made with regard to these agreements on the grounds that they are unconstitutional. In the case of a conflict between international agreements duly brought into domestic law and concerning fundamental rights and freedoms and the laws because of differences in provisions on the same matter, the provisions of international agreements shall prevail.”
Powers and Functions [of the Constitutional Court]

Anyone claiming that a public authority has violated one of his or her fundamental rights and freedoms protected by the Constitution and secured under the European Convention on Human Rights may apply to the Constitutional Court. An application may be lodged only after all ordinary legal remedies have been exhausted.
In an individual application, no review may be carried out in respect of matters that should be examined within the scope of ordinary legal remedies.
The procedures and principles governing individual applications shall be laid down by law.
Decisions of the Constitutional Court
“The decisions of the Constitutional Court are final ...

Decisions of the Constitutional Court shall be published immediately in the Official Gazette, and shall be binding on the legislative, executive and judicial bodies, administrative authorities, and natural and legal persons.
Law no. 6216 on the establishment and rules of procedure of the Constitutional Court
55. The relevant provisions of Law no. 6216 provide:

“(1) Anyone claiming that a public authority has violated one of his or her fundamental rights and freedoms protected by the Constitution and secured under the European Convention on Human Rights and the Protocols thereto that have been ratified by Türkiye may apply to the Constitutional Court.
(2) An individual application may be lodged only after the exhaustion of all the administrative and judicial remedies provided for by law in relation to the measure, act or omission complained of.

“(1) Following the examination of a case on its merits, a decision shall be given as to whether or not a right of the applicant has been violated. Case-law of the Constitutional Court
Case of Kadri Enis Berberoğlu (no. 3)

57. On 21 January 2021 in Kadri Enis Berberoğlu (no. 3), B. No. 2020/32949, the Constitutional Court assessed the consequences of a failure to implement a previous judgment it had given regarding the same applicant – an opposition MP – in which it had found a violation of that applicant’s rights to liberty and security, to stand for election and to engage in political activity under Articles 19 and 67 of the Constitution respectively (Kadri Enis Berberoğlu (no. 2), B. No. 2018/20030). Although the Constitutional Court had transmitted the file to the Istanbul Assize Court for the criminal proceedings against the applicant to be reopened and stayed, the Assize Court had refused to implement the judgment. The Constitutional Court stated that its decisions were final and binding on all judicial authorities under Article 153 of the Constitution and section 66 of Law no. 6216 (see paragraph 54 and 55 above), that its decisions were binding without exception and that lower courts had no discretion to review its decisions or to refuse to implement them. However, the Istanbul Assize Court had failed to implement its previous judgment, despite its clear obligation under section 50 of Law no. 6216 to put an end to the violation found by the Constitutional Court and to redress the effects of the violation. The Constitutional Court found that the failure to implement its previous judgment constituted a fresh violation of the applicant’s rights under Articles 19 and 67 of the Constitution.

58. The Constitutional Court also stated that the obligation to implement its judgments flowed directly from the supremacy and binding force of the Constitution, and that permitting lower courts to disregard a judgment would make the individual application mechanism ineffective and would jeopardise legal certainty, the separation of powers, and the rule of law. The rule of law was not a matter of rhetoric. Any failure to implement the decisions of the Constitutional Court, for whatever reason, in the face of the clear provision of Article 153 of the Constitution, would amount to a grave violation of the principle of the rule of law and of the constitutional order founded upon that principle. No legal system could tolerate arbitrary decisions which, by means of various pretexts and law-defying attitudes and conduct, led to violations of individuals’ fundamental rights and freedoms and to the continuation of existing violations, and which thereby amounted to defiance of the constitutional legal order. It was therefore evident that, in a State governed by the rule of law, failure to implement constitutional provisions gave rise, for those concerned, to criminal, administrative and civil liability.
59. Subsequently, on an unspecified date, the Istanbul Assize Court reopened the criminal proceedings against the applicant and stayed them, in line with the Constitutional Court’s judgment.
Cases of Ömer Gergerlioğlu and Leyla Güven

60. In Ömer Gergerlioğlu (B. No. 2019/10634, 1 July 2021), the Constitutional Court examined the conviction of an opposition MP for disseminating propaganda in favour of a terrorist organisation contrary to section 7 § 2 of Law no. 3713, and the ensuing termination of his parliamentary mandate. The Constitutional Court found violations of the applicant’s right to freedom of expression and his right to stand for election and to engage in political activity. It assessed, inter alia, the legality of Article 14 of the Constitution (see paragraph 53 above), noting that the trial court’s interpretation of that provision (by virtue of the reference in Article 83 § 2 to Article 14) had enabled the continuation of criminal proceedings. It noted that the activities which Article 14 was intended to prevent were not limited to criminal offences; the provision had a broad scope encompassing all activities carried out for certain purposes, whether or not they amounted to a criminal offence. In view of the general wording of Article 14, and in the absence of any constitutional or legal provisions clarifying the scope of the activities it covered, it was not possible for a court to interpret the exception to parliamentary immunity provided by Article 83 § 2. The Constitutional Court further held that both Articles 83 and 14 could fulfil their constitutional function only if interpreted so as to protect democracy and fundamental rights. However, not only had the domestic courts failed to take that approach, there had also been no substantive or procedural rules capable of guiding them to do so.

61. In Leyla Güven (B. No. 2018/26689, 7 April 2022), which concerned the conviction of an opposition MP for membership of a terrorist organisation, the resulting lifting of her parliamentary immunity and her pre-trial detention, the Constitutional Court found violations of her right to personal liberty and security as well as her right to stand for election and to engage in political activity. Reiterating its findings in Gergerlioğlu as regards the legality of Article 14 of the Constitution, the Constitutional Court held that the broadly worded and indeterminate nature of that provision, when read in conjunction with Article 83 § 2, did not satisfy the constitutional requirements of clarity and foreseeability.
Case-law of the Court of Cassation

62. On 26 October 2022 (E. 2020/16-462, K. 2022/671) the plenary criminal divisions of the Court of Cassation examined whether the offence with which the accused was charged – aiding and abetting an armed terrorist organisation, which was later reclassified as supporting a terrorist organisation – fell within the exception to parliamentary immunity in Article 83 § 2 of the Constitution with reference to Article 14. Referring to the previous case-law of one of its criminal divisions, the Court of Cassation noted that disseminating propaganda in favour of a terrorist organisation had consistently been regarded by the Court of Cassation as falling within the scope of Article 14 and thus being an exception to parliamentary immunity. Nevertheless, it then referred to the Constitutional Court’s judgment in Leyla Güven (B. No. 2018/26689 – see paragraph 61 above), in which, following Gergerlioğlu (see paragraph 60 above), the Constitutional Court had held that the exception to parliamentary immunity with reference to Article 14 lacked clarity and foreseeability. Referring to Article 153 of the Constitution (see paragraph 54 above), the plenary criminal divisions stated that it was indisputable that the Constitutional Court judgments – including those delivered in individual applications – were binding and gave guidance for future decision-making. The plenary criminal divisions therefore quashed the conviction on the ground that the lower court had failed to deal with the applicant’s application for the suspension of the proceedings on account of his parliamentary immunity.

63. On 4 April 2023 (E.2023/3102, K.2023/966), the Third Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation examined a prosecution for offences allegedly committed before the accused’s election as an MP. Decisions on individual applications given by the Constitutional Court during pending criminal proceedings may create a conflict of jurisdiction; however, findings of violations of fundamental rights could not be disregarded by trial courts, particularly where violations are grounds for retrial. Emphasising the importance of making restitution for violations of fundamental rights and the principle of the unity of the legal order, the Court of Cassation concluded that the scope of the phrase “situations referred to in Article 14” in Article 83 § 2 must be interpreted and determined in line with the Constitutional Court’s binding case-law.

Emphasising that an individual application was a subsidiary action and it was the primary responsibility of ordinary courts to remedy violations of rights protected under the Constitution and the Convention, the Court of Cassation concluded that such decisions must be taken into account in pending proceedings and that, in order to avoid a further violation, the disputed judgment should be quashed.

Commissioner for Human Rights

65. Following her visit to Türkiye between 1 and 5 July 2019, the then Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe published a report on 19 February 2020 (CommDH(2020)1). In it, she raised concerns about structural deficiencies in the judicial system which affected the independence of the judiciary. She observed that the composition of the Council of Judges and Prosecutors allowed all its members to be appointed by the President or Parliament, without safeguards ensuring pluralism or election by other judges, contrary to European standards. She further noted reports of arbitrary transfers of judges who had made rights-based decisions, the appointment of judges with known biases to politically sensitive cases, and case allocation practices suggesting interference, all of which reinforced concerns about the vulnerability of the judiciary to political influence. The Commissioner also emphasised that public statements by members of the executive and legislature criticising the courts and commenting on ongoing cases, often in disregard of the presumption of innocence, were liable to undermine judicial independence and to influence judicial decision-making. In this context, she referred to the Court’s judgments in Selahattin Demirtaş v. Turkey (no. 2) ([GC], no. 14305/17, 22 December 2020) and Kavala v. Turkey (no. 28749/18, 10 December 2019), in which it held that statements by high-ranking officials could corroborate allegations that orders for detention had been made for an ulterior purpose.

The Commissioner further stated that serious concerns had been raised about the effectiveness of the Constitutional Court individual application mechanism, particularly in sensitive detention cases. She noted that the failure of the lower courts to implement Constitutional Court judgments – most notably in the case of Mehmet Altan, who had remained in detention for some months despite the finding of a violation – had led the Court to question the effectiveness of the individual application to the Constitutional Court as a remedy. She further observed that prosecutors and lower court judges had continued to disregard the Constitutional Court’s clear case-law without facing any consequences. In her view, the lower courts’ resistance undermined the binding force of the Constitutional Court’s judgments and weakened the effectiveness of the individual application system within the constitutional order.

As regards the situation of human-rights defenders, the Commissioner stated that in Kavala, cited above, the Court had found for the first time that criminal proceedings against a human-rights defender had been pursued for an ulterior purpose, namely, not only to silence the applicant but also to discourage the work of human-rights defenders in general, and that the prosecution had relied on entirely lawful and legitimate activities. She further considered that the same concerns applied to Kavala’s co-defendants in the Gezi trial. She concluded that judicial proceedings conducted so as to target civil society actors formed part of a sustained and concerted pressure on human-rights defenders, aimed at silencing them and preventing them from reporting on ongoing human rights violations, and that those judicial actions had produced a palpable chilling effect in Türkiye.

When other state authorities adopt new individual acts, they must take into account the legal reasoning set out in the Constitutional Court’s decisions...

151. Many national constitutions contain an obligation to respect international and supranational law. In those cases, national constitutional courts act not only as guardians of the national constitutional principles, but also as guardians of international and supranational law within the national legal order. In the European continent, many constitutional courts are required to implement human rights and other constitutional principles as protected by the ECHR as interpreted by the decisions of the ECtHR.”
ALLEGED VIOLATION OF ARTICLE 5 § 1 OF THE CONVENTION

70. The applicant complained that his continued detention following conviction, despite his election as an MP and the Constitutional Court’s findings of a violation of his right to liberty and security, was not lawful and amounted to an arbitrary deprivation of liberty. In that connection, he argued that the Court of Cassation had unlawfully interpreted Articles 14 and 83 of the Constitution (see paragraph 53 above), which could only be interpreted by the Constitutional Court, and that it had rejected his applications for release, disregarding his parliamentary immunity.
The applicant relied on Articles 5, 6 and 7 of the Convention.

71. The Court, being the master of the characterisation to be given in law to the facts of the case (see Radomilja and Others v. Croatia [GC], nos. 37685/10 and 22768/12, §§ 110-26, 20 March 2018) considers that the applicant’s complaint falls to be examined only under Article 5 § 1 (a) of the Convention, which reads as follows:
“1. Everyone has the right to liberty and security of person. No one shall be deprived of his liberty save in the following cases and in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law:
(a) the lawful detention of a person after conviction by a competent court;

72. The Government submitted that the applicant’s complaint under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention was inadmissible. In that respect, they relied on their submissions with regard to the merits of that complaint (see paragraph 77 below).
73. The applicant contested that argument.

74. The Court considers that the applicant’s complaint regarding the lawfulness of his continued detention raises complex issues of fact and law, which cannot be determined without an examination of the merits of his case. It moreover finds that this complaint is neither manifestly ill-founded nor inadmissible on any other grounds listed in Article 35 of the Convention. It must therefore be declared admissible.

75. The applicant maintained that following his election as an MP (see paragraph 12 above), the Court of Cassation had failed to release him and to stay the criminal proceedings against him, although it should have done so in line with Article 83 of the Constitution. Moreover, the Court of Cassation had persisted with its failure to release him following the Constitutional Court’s findings of a violation of his rights and orders for his release, as well as the reopening and stay of the criminal proceedings against him. As a result of the unlawful and politically motivated decisions of the Court of Cassation, he remained in detention. His continued detention despite the Constitutional Court’s findings of a violation of his right to liberty and security was therefore unlawful and arbitrary.

76. The applicant specified that the present application pertained solely to his continued detention following his election as an MP despite the Constitutional Court’s judgments ordering his release, and not to the criminal proceedings immediately before his election which resulted in his conviction.

77. The Government pointed out that the applicant had been convicted and was being held in detention having been sentenced by the Istanbul Assize Court to eighteen years’ imprisonment (see paragraphs 8-9 above), and that the conviction and sentence had been upheld by the Court of Cassation (see paragraph 25 above). Although the Constitutional Court had decided that the criminal proceedings against the applicant should be reopened, in Turkish law the proceedings could only be reopened if the application to reopen them was approved by the court concerned. In the present case, the Court of Cassation had not granted that approval, and the applicant’s conviction remained in place. The Government concluded therefore that the applicant’s continued detention was lawful and did not raise an issue under Article 5 § 1 (a) of the Convention.

78. Given that the applicant specifically stated that the present case only concerned his continued detention following his election as an MP and the failure to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgments in his favour (see paragraph 76 above; compare and contrast Kavala v. Türkiye (no. 2) [GC], no. 2170/24, § 227, 25 August 2026), the Court will confine its examination of the complaint under Article 5 § 1 (a) of the Convention to that matter. It will therefore not deal with the question of whether or not the Istanbul Assize Court’s order to detain the applicant following his conviction of aiding an attempt to overthrow the government or to prevent it from performing its functions under Article 312 of the Criminal Code was lawful (see paragraph 9 above; contrast Kavala (no. 2), cited above, §§ 241-48).

79. Article 5 of the Convention is, together with Articles 2, 3 and 4, in the first rank of the fundamental rights that protect the physical security of the individual, and as such its importance is paramount. Its key purpose is to prevent arbitrary or unjustified deprivations of liberty (see Denis and Irvine v. Belgium [GC], nos. 62819/17 and 63921/17, § 123, 1 June 2021, with further references).

80. Sub-paragraphs (a) to (f) of Article 5 § 1 of the Convention contain an exhaustive list of permissible grounds for the deprivation of liberty, and no deprivation of liberty will be lawful unless it falls within one of those grounds. Only a narrow interpretation of the exhaustive list of permissible grounds for deprivation of liberty is consistent with the aim of Article 5, namely to ensure that no one is arbitrarily deprived of his or her liberty (ibid., § 124).

81. The word “after” in sub-paragraph (a) does not simply mean that the detention must follow the “conviction” in point of time: in addition, the “detention” must result from, “follow and depend upon” or occur “by virtue of” the “conviction”. In short, there must be a sufficient causal connection between the two. However, with the passage of time the link between the initial conviction and the extension of the deprivation of liberty will gradually become less strong. The causal link required under sub-paragraph (a) might eventually be broken if a position were reached in which a decision not to release a person, or to re-detain a person, was based on grounds that were inconsistent with the objectives of the sentencing court, or on an assessment that was unreasonable in terms of those objectives. Where that was the case a detention that was lawful at the outset would be transformed into a deprivation of liberty that was arbitrary and therefore incompatible with Article 5 (see Del Río Prada v. Spain [GC], no. 42750/09, § 124, ECHR 2013).

82. Any deprivation of liberty must, in addition to falling within one of the exceptions set out in sub-paragraphs (a) to (f) of Article 5 § 1, be “lawful”. Where the “lawfulness” of detention is in issue, including the question of whether “a procedure prescribed by law” has been followed, the Convention refers essentially to domestic law, but also, where appropriate, to other relevant legal standards, including those which have their source in international law (see Medvedyev and Others v. France [GC], no. 3394/03, § 79, ECHR 2010, and Toniolo v. San Marino and Italy, no. 44853/10, § 44, 26 June 2012). In all cases, the Convention establishes an obligation to conform to the substantive and procedural rules of the laws concerned, but also requires that any deprivation of liberty is compatible with the purpose of Article 5, namely, to protect the individual from arbitrariness (see Medvedyev and Others, cited above, § 79).

83. The Court stresses that where deprivation of liberty is concerned, it is particularly important that the general principle of legal certainty is satisfied. It is therefore essential that the conditions for deprivation of liberty under domestic and/or international law are clearly defined and that the law itself is foreseeable in its application, so that it meets the standard of “lawfulness” set by the Convention, a standard which requires that all law is sufficiently precise to avoid any risk of arbitrariness and to allow the citizen – if need be, with appropriate advice – to foresee, to a degree that is reasonable in the circumstances of the case, the consequences which a given action may entail (see, among other authorities, Medvedyev and Others, cited above, § 80, with further references).
Application of those principles to the present case

84. In the present case, the Court notes that the applicant was deprived of his liberty after conviction by a competent court, namely, after the Istanbul Assize Court’s judgment of 25 April 2022, in which that court convicted him of aiding an attempt to overthrow the government or to prevent it from performing its functions under Articles 39 and 312 of the Criminal Code and sentenced him to eighteen years’ imprisonment (see paragraphs 8-9 above). His detention was therefore explicitly covered by Article 5 § 1 (a) of the Convention (see Khamtokhu and Aksenchik v. Russia [GC], nos. 60367/08 and 961/11, § 55, 24 January 2017). As noted above, for the purposes of the present case, the Court will not deal with whether the applicant’s detention was lawful at the outset, but will establish whether his continued detention following his election as an MP on 14 May 2023 (see paragraph 12 above) was lawful within the meaning of Article 5 § 1 (a) of the Convention (see paragraph 78 above).

85. The Court observes that following his election, the applicant requested the recognition of his parliamentary immunity and to be released, with reference to the Constitutional Court’s case-law on the matter and the Court of Cassation’s previous decisions regarding the binding nature of the Constitutional Court’s decisions (see paragraph 13 above). On 13 July 2023 the Court of Cassation rejected that request. It found that the applicant’s situation fell within the scope of Article 14 of the Constitution, which provided an exception to parliamentary immunity by virtue of Article 83 § 2 (see paragraph 53 above), and that the Constitutional Court’s previous finding that Article 14 was not foreseeable could not be followed as that court could not decide an individual application so as to render a constitutional provision unenforceable. The Court of Cassation therefore concluded that the applicant was not entitled to parliamentary immunity and that the Assize Court’s decision regarding his conviction remained valid (see paragraphs 14‑17 above). On 28 September 2023 the Court of Cassation upheld the Assize Court’s decision and finalised the applicant’s conviction (see paragraphs 20 and 25 above).

86. The Constitutional Court heard the individual application made by the applicant following the Court of Cassation’s decision of 13 July 2023 and reiterated its findings from previous cases raising a similar issue (see paragraphs 60-61 above). Once again, it found that Article 14 of the Constitution was not foreseeable. It held that the applicant’s continued detention following his election as an MP was not prescribed by law and was in violation of his right to liberty and security (see paragraphs 26-29 above). Although the initial reason for his detention had been a sentence pronounced after conviction, given that he had subsequently been elected as an MP and should have benefited from parliamentary immunity, the connection between his conviction and his deprivation of liberty had been severed. The Constitutional Court concluded that there was therefore no legal basis for the applicant’s continued detention (see paragraph 28 above). The Court finds that this conclusion amounts in substance to an acknowledgment that the applicant’s deprivation of liberty was in breach of Article 5 § 1 of the Convention (compare Mehmet Hasan Altan v. Turkey, no. 13237/17, § 129, 20 March 2018, and Şahin Alpay v. Turkey, no. 16538/17, § 108, 20 March 2018).

87. Although the Constitutional Court ordered that the applicant must be released and the criminal proceedings reopened and stayed in order to provide redress for the violation of his right to liberty and security (see paragraph 29 above), the Court of Cassation refused to implement that judgment, for the same reasons it had given in its decision of 13 July 2023. It found that the Constitutional Court had exceeded the limits of its jurisdiction by acting as a fourth-instance court, and went so far as to file a criminal complaint against the Constitutional Court judges who had voted in favour of finding a violation of the applicant’s rights (see paragraphs 32-34 above). The Constitutional Court’s finding of a violation of the applicant’s right to liberty and security in the second individual application and its repeated order for the applicant’s release and the reopening and suspension of the criminal proceedings (see paragraphs 37-39 above) were equally not implemented by the Court of Cassation (see paragraph 42 above).

88. The Court notes that in persistently refusing to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgments, as well as in its press statement of 10 November 2023 (see paragraph 35 above), the Court of Cassation emphasised that there was no hierarchy among the superior courts in the Turkish legal system and that the Constitutional Court had no power to impose its own interpretation of legal provisions on appellate courts. In that connection, the Court observes that in a previous decision the plenary criminal divisions of the Court of Cassation (see paragraph 62 above), as well as the Third Criminal and Second Civil Divisions in other decisions (see paragraphs 63-64 above), reached a completely different conclusion from that in the present case, both as regards whether the Constitutional Court decisions (including those made on individual applications) were binding and as regards the weight to be given to the Constitutional Court’s case-law on the interpretation of Articles 14 and 83 of the Constitution. The Court notes, however, that although the applicant had referred to the plenary criminal divisions’ decision in his initial request for release following his election (see paragraph 13 above) and all of those decisions had been referred to in the Constitutional Court’s decision of 21 December 2023 (see paragraph 39 above), the Court of Cassation did not make any reference to them. It therefore failed to clarify why it had departed from the principles previously set out by the plenary criminal divisions, which it had followed in its earlier decisions.

89. The Court notes that the Government did not address the discrepancy between the superior courts’ interpretation of the constitutional provisions concerned and of the effect of the Constitutional Court decisions, and simply maintained that the applicant’s continued detention was lawful, as his conviction remained valid unless the Court of Cassation approved the Constitutional Court’s judgment that the proceedings should be reopened (see paragraph 77 above). The Court finds it difficult to follow that reasoning, which presupposes that the Constitutional Court’s decisions as to the remedy for the violations it had found would be subject to an approval by the courts concerned. This is not in keeping with either the Court’s case-law regarding the effects of the decisions delivered by the Constitutional Court (see Uzun v. Turkey (dec.), §§ 66-67, no. 10755/13, 30 April 2013, and Koçintar v. Turkey (dec.), no. 77429/12, §§ 40-44, 1 July 2014) or the Government’s observations in previous cases before the Court (see Mehmet Hasan Altan, cited above, § 136, and Şahin Alpay, cited above, § 115). Nor is it consistent with the Court of Cassation’s own case-law, referred to above (see paragraphs 62-64 above).

90. The Court notes that, by virtue of Articles 148 and 153 of the Constitution and sections 45 and 66 of Law no. 6216 (see paragraphs 54-55 above), the Constitutional Court is the supreme judicial authority competent to give a binding interpretation of the constitutional guarantees of individual rights, such as the right to liberty and personal integrity (see Mehmet Hasan Altan, cited above, § 139, and compare Nasrulloyev v. Russia, no. 656/06, § 74, 11 October 2007). It conducts proceedings in a different legal context from that of the ordinary courts (see, mutatis mutandis, Ilnseher v. Germany [GC], nos. 10211/12 and 27505/14, § 270, 4 December 2018, and Selahattin Demirtaş v. Türkiye (no. 4), no. 13609/20, § 153, 8 July 2025). In that regard, the Court has previously found that the Turkish legislature had demonstrated its intention to give the Constitutional Court jurisdiction to find violations of Convention provisions and appropriate powers to provide redress for those violations (see Uzun, cited above, § 64). In Uzun (cited above, § 66), and, with regard to complaints under Article 5 of the Convention, in Koçintar (cited above, § 43), the Court took account of Article 153 § 6 of the Constitution which provides that decisions of the Constitutional Court are binding on the legislature, the executive and the judiciary, administrative authorities, and natural and legal persons. It concluded that, in principle, no issues regarding the implementation of Constitutional Court judgments should arise in Türkiye (ibid.).

91. In Mehmet Hasan Altan and Şahin Alpay (both cited above, § 139 and § 118, respectively) – both of which concerned the courts’ failures to release the applicants from pre-trial detention following the Constitutional Court’s findings of violations of their right to liberty and security – the Court found that the reasons given by the trial courts for rejecting the applicants’ release, following a “final” and “binding” judgment delivered by the supreme constitutional judicial authority, could not satisfy the requirements of Article 5 § 1 of the Convention. It concluded that for another court to call into question the powers conferred on a constitutional court to give final and binding judgments on individual applications ran counter to the fundamental principles of the rule of law and legal certainty (see also Kavala (no. 2), cited above, § 132), which were inherent in the protection afforded by Article 5 of the Convention and were the cornerstones of the guarantees against arbitrariness (for the relevant principles, see paragraphs 82-83 above).

92. In that connection, the Court also reiterates that detention based on provisions which have been interpreted by the domestic authorities in an inconsistent and mutually exclusive manner would not have adequate safeguards against arbitrariness. Such provisions would not be either precise or foreseeable in their application and would fall short of the “quality of law” standard required under the Convention (compare Jėčius v. Lithuania, no. 34578/97, § 59, ECHR 2000-IX, and Nasrulloyev, cited above, § 77). The Court considers that – as pointed out by the dissenting judge at the Fourth Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation (see paragraph 19 above) – as a result of the discrepancy between the superior courts’ interpretations of the legal provisions on which the applicant’s continued detention following his election was based, a question of foreseeability also arises in the present case. That question of foreseeability is further exacerbated by the discrepancy in the Court of Cassation’s own case-law (see paragraph 88 above), which resulted from the Third Criminal Division’s departure from the principles set out by the plenary criminal divisions to ensure consistency in case-law (contrast Beian v. Romania (no. 1), no. 30658/05, § 35, ECHR 2007-V (extracts)) and which was contrary to the principle of legal certainty (ibid., §§ 37-39).

93. In view of the above, in particular the power of the Constitutional Court to review the lawfulness of detention (see paragraph 90 above) and its consistent interpretation of the lack of foreseeability of the legal provisions at issue (see paragraph 86 above), the Court sees no reason to depart from that court’s conclusions with regard to the unlawfulness of the applicant’s continued detention (compare Mehmet Hasan Altan, cited above, § 129, and Şahin Alpay, cited above, § 108).

94. However, as noted above, following the Constitutional Court’s finding in two separate judgments that the applicant’s right to liberty and security had been violated – which has already been found by the Court to constitute an acknowledgement of a violation of Article 5 § 1 (a) of the Convention (see paragraph 86 above) – the Court of Cassation refused to implement those judgments and to release the applicant. The violation found by the Constitutional Court was therefore not remedied (compare Mehmet Hasan Altan, cited above, § 139, and Şahin Alpay, cited above, § 118).

95. Consequently, the Court finds that the applicant’s continued detention following his election as an MP – despite the Constitutional Court’s clear and unambiguous findings that this was in violation of Article 19 of the Constitution ­– was not “lawful” or “in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law” as required by the right to liberty and security (ibid.).
96. There has accordingly been a violation of Article 5 § 1 of the Convention.
ALLEGED VIOLATION OF ARTICLE 5 § 4 OF THE CONVENTION

97. The applicant complained about the authorities’ failure to implement the Constitutional Court judgments in his favour. He argued that the decisions of the Istanbul Assize Court and the Court of Cassation declining to implement the Constitutional Court’s orders had demonstrated that an application to the Constitutional Court could no longer be considered an effective remedy. In that respect he relied on Articles 5 § 4 and 6 § 1 of the Convention.

98. The Court reiterates that, in matters of deprivation of liberty, Article 5 § 4 lays down specific procedural guarantees which are distinct from those enshrined in Article 6 § 1. Even assuming that Article 6 § 1 is applicable under its civil limb, Article 5 § 4 constitutes a lex specialis in relation to that provision (see Manzano Diaz v. Belgium, no. 26402/17, § 26, 18 May 2021, with further references).
