Being the master of the characterisation to be given in law to the facts of the case (see Radomilja and Others, cited above, §§ 110-26), the Court holds that the applicant’s complaint should be examined only under Article 5 § 4 of the Convention, which reads as follows:

“4. Everyone who is deprived of his liberty by arrest or detention shall be entitled to take proceedings by which the lawfulness of his detention shall be decided speedily by a court and his release ordered if the detention is not lawful.”

99. The Government referred to the Court’s case-law and argued that when detention was the result of a judgment delivered at the end of court proceedings – as was the case in the present application – no further review within the meaning of Article 5 § 4 of the Convention was required. This was because the judgment already involved a review of the legality of the detention. They therefore considered that the complaint was inadmissible.
100. The applicant argued that Article 5 § 4 was applicable to his case.

101. The Court notes that while they relied on the case-law of the Court, the Government did not clearly raise any objection as regards the applicability of Article 5 § 4 of the Convention in the present case. It finds, however, that the question concerns compatibility ratione materiae of the complaint which goes to the Court’s jurisdiction and which it must examine of its own motion (see, mutatis mutandis, Béláné Nagy v. Hungary [GC], no. 53080/13, § 71, 13 December 2016).

102. The Court reiterates that, as pointed out by the Government, Article 5 § 4 would in principle be redundant with respect to detention under Article 5 § 1 (a), since judicial control of the deprivation of liberty has already been incorporated into the original conviction and sentence (see, among others, Stoichkov v. Bulgaria, no. 9808/02, § 64, 24 March 2005; Gavril Yosifov v. Bulgaria, no. 74012/01, § 57, 6 November 2008; and Etute v. Luxembourg, no. 18233/16, § 25, 30 January 2018). However, whenever fresh issues affecting the lawfulness of such detention arise, Article 5 § 4 comes back into play (see Stoichkov, cited above, § 65). The Court has found that Article 5 § 4 was applicable even after a conviction when the legality of the detention depended on factors which were not incorporated in the original conviction and sentence (ibid., with further references; see also, Gavril Yosifov, cited above, § 59; Ivan Todorov v. Bulgaria, no. 71545/11, § 61, 19 January 2017; and Etute, cited above, § 33).

103. In the present case, the applicant’s detention was indeed the result of his conviction in the Istanbul Assize Court for aiding an attempt to overthrow the government or to prevent it from performing its functions and his sentence of eighteen years’ imprisonment (see paragraphs 8-9 and 84 above). As discussed above, following his conviction at first instance and while the proceedings were still pending appeal before the Court of Cassation, the applicant was elected as an MP in the parliamentary elections and then lodged a request with the Court of Cassation for recognition that he had the benefit of parliamentary immunity under Article 83 of the Constitution (see paragraphs 12-13 above). After the Court of Cassation had dismissed his applications for release and the suspension of the criminal proceedings (see paragraphs 14-19 above), he lodged individual applications with the Constitutional Court (see paragraphs 24 and 36 above). The Court observes that both the applicant’s request to the Court of Cassation and his subsequent individual applications to the Constitutional Court were only concerned with the lawfulness of his continued detention following his election as an MP and the question of whether he would benefit from parliamentary immunity. These issues were independent of and distinct from the issues dealt with by the Istanbul Assize Court when it ordered the applicant’s conviction and detention and, in any event, could not have been examined at that stage as the Assize Court’s judgment preceded the applicant’s election.

104. It follows that Article 5 § 4 of the Convention is applicable in the present case, as the applicant was entitled to have the specific legal issue of his continued detention following his election resolved by a court which met the requirements of that provision (compare Stoichkov, cited above, § 66).
105. The Court finds that this complaint is neither manifestly ill-founded nor inadmissible on any other grounds listed in Article 35 of the Convention. It must therefore be declared admissible.

106. The applicant submitted that both Article 153 § 6 of the Constitution and section 66 of Law no. 6216 provided that the Constitutional Court decisions were binding (see paragraphs 54-55 above). Moreover, the Court had previously concluded that an individual application to the Constitutional Court constituted an effective remedy. Nevertheless, by declining to implement those judgments, the Istanbul Assize Court and the Court of Cassation had rendered that remedy ineffective. He referred to the relevant case-law of the Court and argued that failures on the part of the judicial authorities to implement Constitutional Court judgments increased the doubts about the effectiveness of the remedy directed by that court. The Court had previously found such doubts to be serious.

107. The Government submitted that, in line with the principle of subsidiarity, the introduction of the individual application mechanism to the Constitutional Court had marked a turning point in the protection of fundamental rights and has proved effective in practice, as demonstrated by the statistics on the number of decisions delivered by that court. They noted that the Court of Cassation and the Constitutional Court were two superior courts, the jurisdiction and functioning of which were regulated separately and which did not have a hierarchical relationship. Moreover, under the Constitution, judges were independent in the discharge of their functions and no body or authority could direct them how to exercise their judicial authority. As the individual application system was relatively new, it might give rise to complex issues of legal interpretation, as was the situation in the present case. According to the Government, the difference in the two superior courts’ interpretation of legal provisions, in particular Articles 14 and 83 of the Constitution, was legally defensible and reasonable and should be perceived as a means to develop case-law, which, in turn would contribute to the strengthening of the protection of fundamental rights. In the present case, the applicant had been able to challenge his continued detention in the two superior courts, which had examined his case in detail, providing sufficient reasons for their decisions. There had therefore been no violation of Article 5 § 4 of the Convention.

108. The Court reiterates that Article 5 § 4 entitles detained persons to institute proceedings for a review of compliance with the procedural and substantive conditions which are essential for the “lawfulness”, in Convention terms, of their deprivation of liberty. The notion of “lawfulness” under paragraph 4 of Article 5 has the same meaning as in paragraph 1, such that a detained person is entitled to a review of the “lawfulness” of his detention in the light not only of the requirements of domestic law but also of the Convention, the general principles embodied therein and the aim of the restrictions permitted by Article 5 § 1. Article 5 § 4 does not guarantee a right to judicial review of such a scope as to empower the court, on all aspects of the case including questions of pure expediency, to substitute its own discretion for that of the decision-making authority. The review should, however, be wide enough to bear on those conditions which are essential for the “lawful” detention of a person according to Article 5 § 1 (see Khlaifia and Others v. Italy [GC], no. 16483/12, § 128, 15 December 2016).

109. The reviewing “court” must not have merely advisory functions but must have the competence to “decide” the “lawfulness” of the detention and to order release if the detention is unlawful (ibid., with further references).

110. By virtue of Article 5 § 4, a detainee is entitled to apply to a “court” which has jurisdiction to decide “speedily” whether or not his deprivation of liberty has become “unlawful” in the light of new factors which have emerged subsequently to the initial decision depriving him or her of his or her liberty (see Azimov v. Russia, no. 67474/11, § 152, 18 April 2013).

111. Article 5 § 4 does not compel the Contracting Parties to set up more than one level of jurisdiction for the examination of the lawfulness of detention and for hearing applications for release. Nevertheless, a State which offers a second level of jurisdiction must in principle accord to the detainees the same guarantees on appeal as at first instance, including as regards the speediness of the review by the appellate body of a detention order imposed by a lower court. The same applies to constitutional courts which decide on the legality of detention and order the release of the person concerned if the detention is not lawful (see Ilnseher, cited above, § 254, with further references).

112. The existence of the remedy must be sufficiently certain, not only in theory but also in practice, failing which it will lack the requisite accessibility and effectiveness (see Khlaifia and Others, cited above, § 130).
Application of those principles to the present case

113. The Court has already recognised that the Constitutional Court is the supreme judicial authority with power to give a binding interpretation of the constitutional guarantees of individual rights (see paragraph 90 above). The Court has also observed that when the Constitutional Court gives a remedy for a violation, it should be able, if necessary, to prohibit the authority concerned from continuing to breach the right in question and to order it to restore, as far as possible, the previous situation (status quo ante) (see Uzun, cited above, §§ 63-64). With regard to complaints under Article 5 of the Convention, the Court has noted that where the Constitutional Court finds a violation of the right to liberty and security and the applicant remains in detention, it should transmit its judgment to the court concerned to take “the necessary action”. It has also considered that an individual application to the Constitutional Court is, in principle, capable of leading to the release of the detained person (see Koçintar, cited above, §§ 42-43).

114. In sum, the Court finds that in its examination of the compliance of a detention with the fundamental right to liberty and security, the Constitutional Court reviews, as do the lower courts, the lawfulness of a complainant’s detention and has jurisdiction to order the release of the detained person if it concludes that the detention is unlawful (compare Ilnseher, cited above, § 270; also see Articles 148 and 153 of the Constitution and sections 45 and 50 of Law no. 6216, cited in paragraphs 54-55 above).

115. In the present case, the Constitutional Court examined the lawfulness of the applicant’s detention in the applicant’s first and second individual applications in the light of a new factor which emerged after the Istanbul Assize Court’s decision to detain the applicant, namely, his election as an MP. As found above (see paragraph 86 above), the Constitutional Court carried out that examination in line with its case-law on parliamentary immunity (and the exceptions to it). It concluded that the applicant’s continued detention following his election was not lawful and that it constituted a violation of his right to liberty and security (see paragraphs 28 and 37 above).

116. The Court has already endorsed that conclusion (see paragraph 93 above), which constitutes an acknowledgement of a breach of Article 5 § 1 of the Convention (see paragraph 86 above). It considers that no question arises either as to the Constitutional Court’s power to review the lawfulness of the disputed detention both under national law and from the standpoint of the Convention or as to the quality of that review in the applicant’s case. Moreover, in both the first and second individual applications, the Constitutional Court carried out its review in compliance with the requirement of “speediness” imposed by Article 5 § 4 of the Convention, that is, within a period of three months (see paragraphs 24 and 26 above) and one month (see paragraphs 36-37 above) respectively (compare and contrast Kavala (no. 2), cited above, §§ 122-25 and 127).

117. In both individual applications, after finding a violation of the applicant’s right to liberty and security, the Constitutional Court ordered his release, as well as the reopening and suspension of the criminal proceedings against him, in order to provide redress for the violation found. However, instead of complying with the Constitutional Court’s judgments, the Assize Court – to which the file was transmitted – went on to transfer the file to the Court of Cassation, which it considered to be the court competent to deal with the matter despite the clear reference to the Assize Court in the Constitutional Court’s decision (see paragraphs 29, 31, 39 and 41 above). The Court of Cassation declined to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgments, concluding that the applicant’s detention fell within the scope of the exceptions to parliamentary immunity in Articles 83 § 2 and 14 of the Constitution, and that the Constitutional Court had exceeded its jurisdiction by finding that Article 14 was not foreseeable (see paragraphs 34 and 42 above).

118. The Government argued that Turkish law did not provide for a hierarchy between the superior courts. They submitted that the fact that two superior courts had come to conflicting conclusions did not necessarily result in an issue under Article 5 § 4 of the Convention as the applicant had been given an opportunity to have the lawfulness of his detention reviewed by those courts (see paragraph 107 above). The Court finds however that those submissions fail to take account not only of the legally binding nature of the Constitutional Court’s judgments as provided by Article 153 § 6 of the Constitution and section 66 of Law no. 6216 (see paragraphs 54-55 above), but also of the ultimate purpose of the review foreseen by Article 5 § 4 of the Convention, namely, to have an applicant’s release ordered when detention has been found to be unlawful (see Khlaifia and Others, cited above, § 128).

119. In that regard, the Court refers back to its above-mentioned case-law regarding the effects of the Constitutional Court’s decisions in the context of the individual application mechanism (see paragraph 113 above). It notes that, despite the binding force of Constitutional Court judgments and that court’s power to order the release of the detained person if it concludes that a detention is unlawful, both the Assize Court and the Court of Cassation declined to implement its judgments in the applicant’s individual applications. As a result, the applicant remained in detention despite the Constitutional Court’s findings of a violation of his right to liberty and security and its orders for his release. The Court observes that this continues to be the case at the date of the present judgment, that is, approximately three years after the Constitutional Court delivered its first judgment in the applicant’s case on 25 October 2023 (see paragraph 26 above).

120. In view of the above, the Court finds that, as a result of the failure to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgments, the Turkish legal system failed to provide the applicant with a review of the lawfulness of his detention which could have led to his release as required by Article 5 § 4 of the Convention. The Court emphasises that this conclusion is without prejudice to the nature and the quality of the review carried out by the Constitutional Court, which it has endorsed (see paragraph 116 above). It is also strictly limited to the particular circumstances of the present case and must not be interpreted as calling into question, in general, the effectiveness of an individual application to the Constitutional Court within the domestic legal system (compare Kavala (no. 2), cited above, § 128).
121. There has therefore been a violation of Article 5 § 4 of the Convention.

122. In so far as the applicant argued that the remedy of an individual application to the Constitutional Court could no longer be considered effective (see paragraph 106 above), the Court has recently found in Kavala (no. 2) (cited above, § 130) that the deliberate non-implementation of the Constitutional Court’s judgments is liable to undermine the rule of law and the effectiveness of the individual appeal to that court in cases concerning human rights. As demonstrated by the non-implementation of the Constitutional Court’s judgments in the present case this situation does not result from intrinsic shortcomings relating to the functioning of the Constitutional Court or to its ability to find violations, but instead sheds light on a serious difficulty arising from the attitude of certain lower courts with regard to the binding force of that court’s judgments (ibid.). In that regard, as also noted in Kavala (no. 2) (cited above, § 131), the Court takes note of the Constitutional Court’s analysis that the non-implementation of its decisions was likely not only to undermine individual and societal confidence in the rule of law, but also to compromise the constitutional order (see paragraph 38 above) and the Commissioner for Human Rights’ finding that such a situation represents serious rule-of-law backsliding and weakens the effectiveness of the individual application in cases that concern human rights (see paragraphs 65-67 above).

123. The Court reiterates that, since the Constitutional Court is the cornerstone of the national system for protecting the rights and freedoms enshrined in both the Constitution and the Convention, full compliance with that court’s binding judgments is essential (see Kavala (no. 2), cited above, § 132). As noted in paragraph 91 above, for another domestic court to call into question the powers conferred on a constitutional court to deliver final and binding judgments on individual applications runs counter to the fundamental principles of the rule of law and legal certainty (see Kavala (no. 2), cited above, § 132, with further references). The failure to enforce the Constitutional Court’s rulings is likely not only to compromise that court’s authority, but also to undermine, more generally, the judicial protection of fundamental rights (ibid.). This being said, for the purposes of the present case, the Court reiterates that its finding that the remedy of an individual application before the Constitutional Court did not provide the applicant with a review within the meaning of Article 5 § 4 of the Convention remains strictly limited to the specific circumstances of the present case and does not call into question the general effectiveness of that remedy (see paragraph 120 above).
ALLEGED VIOLATION OF ARTICLE 3 of Protocol No. 1 to THE CONVENTION

124. The applicant complained that as a result of his continued detention and the Court of Cassation’s failure to implement the judgments of the Constitutional Court in which it had found that his right to stand for election had been violated, he had not been able to take up his seat in Parliament. He relied on Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. Being the master of the characterisation to be given in law to the facts of the case (see Radomilja and Others, cited above, §§ 110-26), the Court considers that the applicant’s complaint falls to be examined only under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, which provides:

“The High Contracting Parties undertake to hold free elections at reasonable intervals by secret ballot, under conditions which will ensure the free expression of the opinion of the people in the choice of the legislature.”

125. The Government considered that the applicant’s complaint under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention was inadmissible. In that respect, they relied on their submissions regarding the merits of that complaint (see paragraph 129 below).
126. The applicant did not make any submissions with regard to the admissibility of this complaint.

127. The Court considers that this complaint raises complex issues of fact and law which cannot be determined without an examination on the merits. It moreover finds that it is neither manifestly ill-founded nor inadmissible on any other grounds listed in Article 35 of the Convention. It must therefore be declared admissible.

128. The applicant submitted that the right for an MP to take his or her seat in Parliament served a greater public interest which was inherent to a democratic political system and was therefore protected by constitutional safeguards, including parliamentary immunity. He argued that an unconstitutional interference with his ability to perform his parliamentary functions undermined political representation by the will of the people and prevented voters’ choices from being reflected in the National Assembly. As the Constitutional Court had concluded, the authorities’ failure to allow him to benefit from parliamentary immunity and his resulting continued detention in the absence of a clear and foreseeable legal framework violated his right to stand for election and to engage in political activity. Despite the Constitutional Court’s findings in that regard, the relevant courts had failed to release him and to stay the criminal proceedings against him, as a result of which failure he had not been able to take up his position as an MP.

129. The Government maintained that the Court of Cassation had interpreted the exception to parliamentary immunity provided by Article 83 § 2 of the Constitution with the phrase “cases falling under Article 14” and had found, in line with its consistent case-law, that the offence the applicant had been convicted of – namely, attempting to overthrow the government by force and violence or to prevent it from discharging its functions – fell within the scope of Article 14 of the Constitution. In that regard, the Court of Cassation had referred, in particular, to the explanatory memoranda of Articles 309 and 312 of the Criminal Code and the terrorist offences listed in Law no. 3713 (see paragraph 15 above). In the Government’s opinion, the fact that the legislature had deliberately refrained from making a list of which offences fell within the scope of Article 14 did not render that provision systematically unforeseeable. Moreover, Article 148 § 4 of the Constitution and section 50 § 1 of Law no. 6216 provided, respectively, that the Constitutional Court could not review matters that must be taken into account by courts within the scope of ordinary legal remedies or the appropriateness of an administrative act (see paragraphs 54‑55 above). Referring to the Court’s case-law, the Government stated that many laws were inevitably couched in vague terms and that there was often an inherent element of judicial interpretation. The rule of law required the judicial authorities to identify which offences fell within the scope of Article 14 of the Constitution, having regard to the wording and spirit of the Constitution, as had been done by the Court of Cassation in the present case. They concluded that the offence at issue indeed fell within the scope of Article 14 of the Constitution and that the applicant could not benefit from parliamentary immunity. His detention had been based on a final judicial decision and his parliamentary duty had been terminated when that judicial decision had been read out at the National Assembly (see paragraph 47 above). There had therefore been no violation of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

130. The Court reiterates that democracy constitutes a fundamental element of the “European public order”, and that the rights guaranteed under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 are crucial to establishing and maintaining the foundations of an effective and meaningful democracy governed by the rule of law (see Selahattin Demirtaş (no. 2), cited above, § 382, with further references). The Court has established that, besides the obligation for the High Contracting Party to hold elections under conditions which ensure the free expression of the opinion of the people, Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 also guarantees individual rights, including the right to vote and to stand for election (see Ždanoka v. Latvia [GC], no. 58278/00, § 102, ECHR 2006‑IV), and, once elected, to sit as a member of parliament (see Selahattin Demirtaş (no. 2), cited above, § 386, with further references). The rule of parliamentary immunity, present in most of the Contracting States including Türkiye, is crucial to this guarantee (ibid.).

131. The Court reaffirms that the object and purpose of the Convention require its provisions to be interpreted and applied in such a way as to make their stipulations not theoretical or illusory but practical and effective (see, for example, Grosaru v. Romania, no. 78039/01, § 47, ECHR 2010, with further references). However, the rights guaranteed by Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, which are inherent in the concept of a truly democratic system, would be merely illusory if elected representatives or their voters could be arbitrarily deprived of them at any moment (see Selahattin Demirtaş (no. 2), cited above, § 386, with further references).

132. The rights enshrined in Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 are not absolute. There is room for “implied limitations”, and the Contracting States have a wide margin of appreciation in this sphere. However, it is for the Court to finally determine whether the requirements of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 have been complied with. It has to satisfy itself that any limitations of the exercise of the rights under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 do not curtail those rights to such an extent as to impair their very essence and deprive them of their effectiveness; that they are imposed in pursuit of a legitimate aim; and that the means employed are not disproportionate (ibid., § 387, with further references).

133. In the light of the principle that conditions imposed on the exercise of individual rights guaranteed by Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 may not curtail these rights to such an extent as to impair their very essence and deprive them of their effectiveness, as well as the general Convention requirement that rights must be effective and not illusory, the Court has considered that where restrictions on eligibility to stand for election are provided for by law, the law should satisfy certain minimum requirements as to its quality, such as the requirement of accessibility and foreseeability (see Seyidzade v. Azerbaijan, no. 37700/05, § 33, 3 December 2009, and Kokëdhima v. Albania, no. 55159/16, § 51, 11 June 2024). Furthermore, a disputed measure must have some basis in domestic law and must also be compatible with the rule of law, which is expressly mentioned in the Preamble to the Convention and is inherent in all its Articles (see Selahattin Demirtaş (no. 2), cited above, § 249).

134. Many laws are inevitably couched in terms which, to a greater or lesser extent, are vague, and whose interpretation and application are questions of practice (ibid., § 250). No matter how clearly drafted a legal provision may be, there is an inevitable element of judicial interpretation. There will always be a need for elucidation of doubtful points and for adaptation to changing circumstances (see Kokëdhima, cited above, § 54). The mere fact that a legal provision is capable of more than one construction does not mean that it fails to meet the requirement of “foreseeability” for the purposes of the Convention. The role of adjudication vested in the courts is precisely to dissipate such doubts as remain as to interpretation, taking into account changes in everyday practice (see Selahattin Demirtaş (no. 2), § 253, and Kokëdhima, § 55, both cited above).

135. The Court also reiterates that its power to review compliance with domestic law is limited. It is primarily for the national authorities, notably the courts, to interpret and apply domestic law, even in those fields where the Convention “incorporates” the rules of that law, since the domestic authorities are, in the nature of things, particularly qualified to settle the issues arising in this connection (see Selahattin Demirtaş (no. 2), cited above, § 249). This is particularly true when, as in this instance, the case turns on questions of interpretation of national constitutional law. Unless the interpretation is arbitrary or manifestly unreasonable, the Court’s role is confined to ascertaining whether the effects of that interpretation are compatible with the Convention (see Radomilja and Others, § 149, and Kokëdhima, § 57, both cited above).
Application of those principles to the present case

136. In the present case, it is not disputed that the applicant’s inability to take his seat in Parliament and perform his parliamentary functions because of his continued detention, and the eventual termination of his mandate as an MP on account of his final conviction, constituted an interference with his rights under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. What is in dispute is the foreseeability of the constitutional provisions in question, relating to parliamentary immunity (compare Tomenko v. Ukraine, no. 79340/16, § 106, 10 July 2025) and whether the Court of Cassation was bound to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgments in that regard.

137. The Court takes note of the Government’s submissions regarding the domestic courts’ judicial interpretation of legal provisions and their reference to the Court’s relevant case-law (see paragraph 129 above; for the relevant principles, see paragraphs 134-135 above). However, it observes that, in doing so, the Government referred only to the Court of Cassation’s interpretation of the relevant constitutional provision, namely Article 14 of the Constitution, and not to that of the Constitutional Court. The only reference made by the Government to the Constitutional Court’s assessment of the case was to the provisions of the Constitution setting forth that that court could not examine matters that must be taken into account by courts within the scope of ordinary legal remedies or review the appropriateness of an administrative act. The Court does not consider that reference, which implies that the Constitutional Court went beyond its jurisdiction, to be relevant in the present case. It observes that when it assessed the restrictions caused to the applicant’s right to stand for elections on account of his continued detention and conviction, the Constitutional Court did not act as a fourth-instance body but determined whether those restrictions complied with Article 67 of the Constitution which provided for the right to stand for election and to engage in political activity (see, mutatis mutandis, Mehmet Hasan Altan, cited above, § 163).

138. The Court has already stated that the Constitutional Court was the supreme judicial authority with power to give a binding interpretation of the constitutional guarantees of individual rights (see paragraphs 90, 113, and 123 above; also see, mutatis mutandis, Mehmet Hasan Altan, cited above, § 139). Accordingly, it sees no reason to depart from the Constitutional Court’s findings regarding the unlawfulness of the interference with the applicant’s rights to stand for election and engage in political activities (see paragraphs 26-28 above; compare Paunović and Milivojević v. Serbia, no. 41683/06, § 63, 24 May 2016). In that regard, the Court also notes that the Constitutional Court’s interpretation of the constitutional provision in question was consistent with its previous case-law (see paragraph 86 above) and was based on an assessment from the standpoint of the right to stand for election as provided by both Article 67 of the Constitution and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. Moreover, it finds that the discrepancy between the two superior courts’ interpretations of the provision in question and of the exceptions to parliamentary immunity exacerbates the doubts surrounding the foreseeability of the provision (see a similar conclusion reached by the Court in paragraph 92 above with regard to Article 5 § 1 of the Convention).

139. The Constitutional Court’s power to give a binding interpretation was also acknowledged by both the plenary criminal divisions of the Court of Cassation and by the Third Criminal Division, which examined the applicant’s case, itself (see paragraphs 62-63 above). Nevertheless, neither in its examination of the applicant’s request for his release and the suspension of the criminal proceedings following his election (see paragraph 14 above) nor in its decisions declining to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgments with respect to the applicant (see paragraphs 32-34 and 42 above) did the Third Criminal Division clarify the reasons for its departure from its previous decisions (compare Vujović and Lipa D.O.O. v. Montenegro (no. 2), no. 43050/22, § 107, 27 November 2025, in which the Court examined, in the context of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, the Court of Appeal’s repeated failure to implement the Constitutional Court’s decisions, despite their being binding).

140. In the present case, the Constitutional Court’s binding judgments, in which it found a violation of the applicant’s right to stand for election, required the Court of Cassation to release the applicant and to stay the criminal proceedings against him. As a result of the Court of Cassation’s refusal to implement those judgments, the applicant could not take his seat in Parliament, and his mandate as an MP was eventually terminated on the basis of his conviction (see paragraph 47 above): a conviction resulting from decisions which had previously been found by the Constitutional Court to be unlawful and a violation of the rule of law (see paragraphs 26-28 and 38-39 above). The Constitutional Court later characterised the termination of the applicant’s mandate as an MP as a de facto situation arising from a decision which had previously been found to be devoid of any legal force (see paragraph 49 above).

141. The Court has found, albeit in contexts that are distinguishable from the present one, that the rule of law, one of the fundamental principles of a democratic society, entails a duty on the part of the State and the public authorities to implement judicial orders or decisions against them (compare Petkov and Others v. Bulgaria, nos. 77568/01 and 2 others, §§ 62 and 65, 11 June 2009). It has also found, in relation to the lawfulness of applicants’ continued detention under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention, that for another court to call into question the powers conferred on a constitutional court to give final and binding judgments on individual applications ran counter to the fundamental principles of the rule of law and legal certainty (see Mehmet Hasan Altan, § 139, and Şahin Alpay, § 118, both cited above – paragraph 91 above; also see Kavala (no. 2), cited above, § 132).

142. In view of the above, the Court concludes that the applicant’s inability to take his seat in Parliament and the eventual termination of his parliamentary mandate on account of his conviction and continued detention were incompatible with the rule of law, and therefore unlawful, constituting an unjustified interference not only with his own right to stand for election and to sit in Parliament, but also with the free expression of the will of the people (see, mutatis mutandis, Selahattin Demirtaş (no. 2), § 397, and Tomenko, cited above, § 119).
143. There has therefore been a violation of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.
ALLEGED VIOLATION OF ARTICLE 18 of THE CONVENTION

144. The applicant complained under Article 18 of the Convention that his continued detention and resulting inability to take his seat as an MP had been caused by politically motivated decisions, which had pursued the ulterior purpose of silencing him and preventing him from exercising his parliamentary activities. In that regard, he argued that the Court of Cassation’s decisions declining to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgments had been encouraged by the President of the Republic and other public officials.

145. The Court notes that this complaint relates to a fundamental aspect of the case that has not been addressed above and which merits a separate examination (see, mutatis mutandis, Selahattin Demirtaş (no. 2), cited above, § 401, and Kavala (no. 2), cited above, § 266). It therefore considers that it should be examined under Article 18 of the Convention in conjunction with Article 5 of the Convention and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. Article 18 provides:
“The restrictions permitted under [the] Convention to the said rights and freedoms shall not be applied for any purpose other than those for which they have been prescribed.”

146. The Government considered that Article 18 of the Convention did not have an autonomous role and could only be applied in conjunction with other provisions of the Convention. In their view, given that there was no violation of Article 5 of the Convention or Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, a complaint under Article 18 was incompatible ratione materiae with the provisions of the Convention. In that regard, they also argued that there were no explicit or implicit limitations in Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 that could lead to an examination of the applicant’s complaint under Article 18. The Government further submitted that the applicant’s complaint under this provision was still pending before the Constitutional Court and must therefore be declared inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies. Lastly, they argued that the applicant had failed to submit arguments and evidence to substantiate his complaint that the domestic authorities had pursued aims other than those stated in the Convention.
147. The applicant contested those arguments.
Compatibility ratione materiae

148. While the Government argued that no examination of a complaint under Article 18 of the Convention could be carried out in the absence of a violation under the substantive provision, the Court reiterates that there can be a breach of Article 18 even if there is no breach of the Article in conjunction with which it applies (see Merabishvili v. Georgia, [GC], no. 72508/13, § 288, 28 November 2017). In any event, it notes that it has already found a violation of Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 of the Convention and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention (see paragraphs 96, 121 and 143 above). In so far as the Government argued that Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 had no limitations that would allow the Court to carry out an examination of Article 18 in conjunction with that provision, the Court reiterates that the rights enshrined in Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 are not absolute; there is room for “implied limitations” (see Selahattin Demirtaş (no. 2), cited above, § 387). Given that the complaint under Article 18 is closely linked to the complaints under Article 5 and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, the Court dismisses the Government’s objection of incompatibility ratione materiae (compare Kavala, cited above, § 201, and Tuğluk v. Türkiye, no. 71757/17, § 159, 14 October 2025).
Exhaustion of domestic remedies

149. The general principles with regard to the exhaustion of domestic remedies may be found in Vučković and Others v. Serbia ((preliminary objection) [GC], nos. 17153/11 and 29 others, §§ 69-77, 25 March 2014), Communauté genevoise d’action syndicale (CGAS) v. Switzerland ([GC], no. 21881/20, §§ 138-145, 27 November 2023), and Duarte Agostinho and Others v. Portugal and 32 Others ((dec.) [GC], no. 39371/20, § 215, 9 April 2024). The Court reiterates, in particular, that applicants are required to make normal use of any remedies which are available and sufficient in respect of their Convention grievances. The remedies in question must be sufficiently certain not only in theory but in practice, failing which they will lack the requisite accessibility and effectiveness. To be effective, a remedy must be capable of remedying the disputed state of affairs directly and must offer reasonable prospects of success. The rule of exhaustion is neither absolute nor capable of being applied automatically; in reviewing whether it has been observed it is essential to have regard to the particular circumstances of each individual case. As regards the burden of proof, it is incumbent on the Government claiming non-exhaustion to satisfy the Court that the remedy was an effective one, available in theory and in practice at the relevant time (see Gherghina v. Romania, (dec.) [GC] no. 42219/07, §§ 85-88, 9 July 2015, with further references).

150. The applicant did not raise a separate complaint under Article 18 of the Convention in the first two individual applications he made to the Constitutional Court following his election. He did so only in his subsequent applications, which, at the date of the latest information available to the Court (16 April 2025), were still pending before that court (see paragraphs 44-46 above) and relied solely on Article 18 of the Convention, without raising any corresponding provisions of the Constitution. In that regard, the Court notes that, by virtue of Article 148 of the Constitution and section 45 of Law no. 6216, an individual application may be made to the Constitutional Court for alleged violations of fundamental rights and freedoms in the Convention in so far as they are also protected by the Constitution (see paragraphs 54-55 above, also see Uzun, cited above, § 62). Although the complaint under Article 18 has not yet been considered by the Constitutional Court, in the absence of any corresponding constitutional provisions relied on by the applicant before that court or pointed out by the Government, a question arises both as to that court’s authority to give a binding judgment on Article 18 and as to whether the applicant’s submissions under that Article have already been addressed – at least in substance – in his previous individual applications to the Constitutional Court (see paragraph 27 above for the Constitutional Court’s assessment with regard to the lack of safeguards against politically motivated or unnecessary restrictions on the exercise of parliamentary functions).

151. Nevertheless, in the present case, the Court will not address these questions as it considers in any event that the Government’s objection regarding the exhaustion of domestic remedies should be dismissed for the following reasons. The Court takes note of the reasons given by the Court of Cassation for refusing to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgments on the applicant’s individual applications. It notes in particular that the Court of Cassation challenged the principle that the Constitutional Court’s judgments on individual applications were binding on the other superior courts (see paragraphs 32-35 above). The Court of Cassation further emphasised that reasoning in its decision of 3 January 2024, in which it declined to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgment on the applicant’s second constitutional complaint despite the finding of a violation of the applicant’s right to individual application (see paragraph 42 above). In view of the overt refusal by the Court of Cassation to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgments in the applicant’s case, the Court finds that, in the circumstances of the present case, the remedy provided by the Constitutional Court cannot be considered to offer reasonable prospects of success with regard to the applicant’s complaint under Article 18, which, at the date of the latest available information, was still pending before that court. The applicant therefore cannot be criticised for bringing the Article 18 complaint before the Court without waiting for the judgment of the Constitutional Court. It follows that the Government’s objection under this head must also be dismissed. The Court reaches this conclusion in the specific circumstances of the present case and without prejudice to the effectiveness of the remedy provided by the system of individual applications to the Constitutional Court (for a similar conclusion, see paragraphs 120 and 123 above).

152. As regards the Government’s claim that the applicant had not put forward arguments and evidence to substantiate his complaint, the Court finds that the applicant raised sufficiently detailed arguments (see paragraph 155 below) and notes that he provided it with press articles and other documents reporting the statements made by public officials regarding his case (see paragraphs 50-52 above; contrast Mirgadirov v. Azerbaijan and Turkey, no. 62775/14, § 133, 17 September 2020). The information provided by the applicant was therefore sufficient to enable the Court to determine the nature and scope of the complaint without recourse to any other document (for the relevant principles, see Fu Quan, s.r.o. v. the Czech Republic [GC], no. 24827/14, §§ 145-46, 1 June 2023). It therefore dismisses this objection by the Government as well.
Conclusion on admissibility
153. The Court concludes that this complaint is neither manifestly ill‑founded nor inadmissible on any other grounds listed in Article 35 of the Convention. It must therefore be declared admissible.

154. The applicant complained that his continued detention was politically motivated and pursued an ulterior purpose within the meaning of Article 18 of the Convention in conjunction with Article 5 of the Convention and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, namely, to silence him and to prevent him from participating in parliamentary activities. He argued that the refusal of the domestic authorities to implement the Constitutional Court’s directions for his release and the suspension of the criminal proceedings against him after his election as an MP demonstrated that the authorities had been keeping him in detention deliberately. In his view, this was linked to his political position and his activities as a human rights lawyer involved in socially and politically sensitive cases, including those related to the Gezi Park events (see paragraph 5 above). He further argued that the statements made by public officials, including the President (see paragraphs 50-52 above), which had targeted him, labelled him a “terrorist”, and criticised the Constitutional Court, had had a decisive influence on the domestic courts’ decisions. As a result, the Court of Cassation and the State authorities had adopted a coordinated approach, publicly challenging the powers of the Constitutional Court and insisting that his conviction was final despite the binding decisions of that court in his favour. Moreover, the criminal complaint made by the Court of Cassation against the Constitutional Court judges who had voted in favour of finding a violation in his case (see paragraph 34 above), constituted an unprecedented illustration of the authorities’ determination to resist the Constitutional Court’s judgments and to ensure that he was kept in detention.

155. The Government argued that the applicant had failed to demonstrate that his detention pursued an ulterior purpose within the meaning of Article 18 of the Convention. Relying on the Court’s case-law, they stated that showing a violation of Article 18 had a particularly high evidential threshold and that the Convention system was based on the presumption that public authorities acted in good faith. In their view, the applicant’s reliance on statements made by politicians and public officials was not sufficient to establish bad faith or a hidden agenda on the part of the judicial authorities, particularly in the absence of manifest procedural irregularities or fabricated charges. There had been extensive public debate regarding the case, which had also included views favouring the applicant. Public discussion of the case in the media and by political activists was a normal feature of democratic societies and did not demonstrate that the domestic courts had acted under pressure or pursued an ulterior motive. The Government further maintained that the applicant had been convicted and was detained in execution of a final judgment, that his legal status had been examined in detail by the domestic courts, including the Court of Cassation, and that he had made extensive use of the available domestic remedies, including several applications to the Constitutional Court. The differing interpretations of the Constitutional Court and the Court of Cassation regarding the relevant constitutional provisions reflected a legitimate legal debate between two superior courts rather than political interference.

156. The Court refers to the general principles set out in its judgments in Merabishvili (cited above, § 287-317), Navalnyy v. Russia ([GC], nos. 29580/12 and 4 others, §§ 164-65, 15 November 2018), and Selahattin Demirtaş (no. 2) (cited above, §§ 421-22).

157. In the present case, the Court has concluded that, in view of the Constitutional Court’s binding judgments finding a violation of the applicant’s right to liberty and security and directing his release and the suspension of the criminal proceedings against him, the applicant’s continued detention following his election did not constitute lawful detention after conviction within the meaning of Article 5 § 1 (a) of the Convention and thus was not “in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law” as required by that provision (see paragraph 95 above). The Court has found that the failure to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgments meant that the Turkish legal system failed to provide the applicant with a review mechanism that would lead to his release as required by Article 5 § 4 of the Convention (see paragraph 120 above). It has further concluded that the applicant’s resulting inability to sit in Parliament and the termination of his mandate was not lawful within the meaning of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention (see paragraph 142 above). The Court finds therefore that no issue arises in the present case with respect to the plurality of purposes where a restriction is applied both for an ulterior purpose and a purpose prescribed by the Convention. However, the mere fact that the restriction of the applicant’s rights did not pursue a purpose prescribed by the Convention is not in itself a sufficient basis to conclude that Article 18 has also been violated. It remains for the Court to determine whether there is proof that the authorities’ actions were actually driven by an ulterior purpose (see, mutatis mutandis, Navalnyy, cited above, § 166; Kavala, cited above, §§ 218-19; Selahattin Demirtaş (no. 2), cited above, § 423; and Aliyev v. Azerbaijan, nos. 68762/14 and 71200/14, § 206, 20 September 2018).

158. The Court considers that, in the present case, proof of an ulterior purpose can be established beyond reasonable doubt by assessing the particular circumstances of the case and contextual factors (for a similar approach, see Democracy and Human Rights Resource Centre and Mustafayev v. Azerbaijan, nos. 74288/14 and 64568/16, § 106, 14 October 2021; Zarema Musayeva and Others v. Russia, no. 4573/22, § 87, 28 May 2024; and Selahattin Demirtaş (no. 4), cited above, § 312).

159. The Court observes that there is no dispute between the parties that the applicant is a human-rights defender and a lawyer (see paragraph 5 above). In that regard, it reiterates that it attaches particular importance to the special role of human-rights defenders in promoting and defending human rights, including in close cooperation with the Council of Europe, and their contribution to the protection of human rights in the member States (see Aliyev, § 208, and Democracy and Human Rights Resource Centre and Mustafayev, § 107, both cited above). The Court also observes that the applicant was prosecuted and convicted in the same criminal proceedings as the applicant in Kavala and Kavala (no. 2) (both cited above, §§ 215-32, and §§ 265-79, respectively), in which it found, inter alia, a violation of Article 18 of the Convention in conjunction with Article 5 § 1 of the Convention (compare Azizov and Novruzlu v. Azerbaijan, nos. 65583/13 and 70106/13, § 69, 18 February 2021). His situation cannot therefore be viewed in isolation and should be placed in the context of the detention of other political opponents, human-rights defenders and journalists who have been detained and charged to a large extent with manifestly exaggerated criminal offences against the backdrop of the detention of other political opponents, human-rights defenders and journalists in the respondent State (see, mutatis mutandis, Kavala (no. 2), cited above, § 269, with further references).

160. The Court notes that, as demonstrated by the cases referred to above (see paragraphs 57 and 91 above), the applicant’s case was not the first occasion on which the authorities had declined to implement findings of a violation and orders as to redress from the Constitutional Court regarding the detention of political opponents, human-rights defenders and journalists. In Mehmet Hasan Altan and Şahin Alpay (both cited above, § 139 and § 118, respectively), in which both applicants were journalists, the Court found a violation of Article 5 § 1 on account of the Istanbul Assize Court’s refusal to implement judgments in which the Constitutional Court had found a violation of the applicants’ right to liberty and security, and their continued detention despite final and binding judgments in their favour. In the case of Kadri Enis Berberoğlu (see paragraphs 57-58 above), lodged with the Constitutional Court by an opposition MP, that court had found a fresh violation of the applicant’s right to liberty and security and of his right to stand for election because the Assize Court had failed to implement its directions.

161. Nevertheless, while in Kadri Enis Berberoğlu the lower court had eventually implemented the Constitutional Court’s judgment and stayed the criminal proceedings against the applicant (see paragraph 59 above), in the present case, in its decision of 3 January 2024 the Court of Cassation resisted the Constitutional Court’s judgment on the applicant’s second individual application, despite the finding of an additional violation of his right of individual application on account of its failure to implement the previous judgment in his favour (see paragraph 42 above). The Court observes that that decision declining to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgment for a second time was unprecedented. The failure of the Court of Cassation to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgments meant that the applicant remained in detention despite his election as an MP and was therefore unable to take his seat in Parliament. Moreover, his mandate was terminated when the Court of Cassation’s decision of 3 January 2024 was read out at the National Assembly (see paragraph 47 above; contrast Melia v. Georgia, no. 13668/21, § 137, 7 September 2023, in which the Court did not find an ulterior purpose of removing the applicant from the political scene because the authorities had not restricted his ability to run an election campaign or to carry out his parliamentary mandate, and had suspended criminal proceedings against him in order to allow him to participate properly in the parliamentary elections).

162. The Court observes that when it dismissed the applicant’s application for his release and for the suspension of the criminal proceedings against him on account of his parliamentary immunity and, later on, when it overtly declined to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgments in the applicant’s favour, the Third Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation departed from the principles which had been set by the plenary criminal divisions on the effects of the Constitutional Court judgments. The plenary criminal divisions had established that, notwithstanding the Court of Cassation’s own interpretation of the scope of Article 14 of the Constitution and of the exceptions to parliamentary immunity, it was bound to follow the Constitutional Court’s judgments in which it held that that constitutional provision was not foreseeable, because those judgments were binding by virtue of Article 153 of the Constitution and constituted guidance to be followed in future cases (see paragraph 62 above). The Third Criminal Division had followed those principles in several decisions, including a decision delivered in April 2023 (see paragraph 63 above), that is, only three months before its decision of 13 July 2023, in which it dismissed the applicant’s request for recognition of his parliamentary immunity (see paragraph 14 above). Nevertheless, in the present case, the Third Criminal Division challenged the Constitutional Court’s power to deliver binding judgments on individual applications, without addressing the discrepancy between that approach and the principles which had been established by the plenary criminal divisions and in its own case-law. Both the plenary criminal divisions and, in its earlier decisions, the Third Criminal Division had acknowledged that Constitutional Court judgments were binding and had emphasised the importance of redressing violations of fundamental rights and the principle of the unity of the legal order (see paragraphs 62 and 63 above).

163. The Court finds that the above-mentioned discrepancy in the Court of Cassation’s case-law was significantly exacerbated by the criminal complaint filed by the members of the Third Criminal Division against the Constitutional Court judges who had voted in favour of finding a violation in the applicant’s case (see paragraph 34 above). While the Court has no information as to the possible institution of criminal proceedings against the Constitutional Court judges in question, it finds that the making of that complaint is sufficient in itself to raise a question about the unity of the legal order emphasised in the Court of Cassation’s previous decisions. In that regard, the Court also points to the press statement made by the Court of Cassation two days after the filing of the criminal complaint and the criticisms raised by that court. In its press statement the Court of Cassation portrayed the Constitutional Court’s remedial directions within the individual application mechanism as a fourth-instance examination of appellate courts’ decisions which could potentially lead to chaos in the legal system (see paragraph 35 above).

164. The Court notes those arguments advanced by the Court of Cassation with concern. It has already found that Constitutional Court judgments are binding on all State bodies, including judicial authorities by virtue of Article 153 § 6 of the Constitution and section 66 of Law no. 6216 (see paragraphs 90 and 113 above). The implementation of Constitutional Court judgments is therefore a requirement that flows from the principle of legal certainty and the rule of law (in that regard, see Kavala (no. 2), cited above, §§ 130-32). As was also pointed out by the plenary criminal divisions of the Court of Cassation (see paragraph 62 above), that requirement applies irrespective of the differences in the superior courts’ interpretation of legal provisions. Once the Constitutional Court had concluded that the applicant’s continued detention and the interference with his right to stand for election were not lawful and clearly stated the steps to be taken to remedy those violations, both the Assize Court and the Court of Cassation were bound to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgments and to provide redress as directed by the Constitutional Court. In that respect, the Court reiterates that a failure to implement Constitutional Court judgments not only has serious repercussions for the individual rights of those concerned, as was the case for the applicant, but also risks damaging the rule of law and the constitutional order (see paragraphs 122-123 above). In the present case, the Court of Cassation’s refusal to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgment on the applicant’s second application despite an additional finding of a violation of the applicant’s right of individual application – which, as noted above, was unprecedented (see paragraph 161 above) – displays a departure from those principles. The Court considers that such a departure cannot be explained solely by a difference of interpretation by the superior courts, as was claimed by the Government (see paragraph 155 above), and that it raises a question as to its purpose.

165. In that regard, the Court also takes note of the statements made by the President of the Republic and his Chief Advisor, M.U., supporting the Court of Cassation’s stance in the applicant’s case and raising similar criticisms regarding the Constitutional Court’s findings, in particular as regards parliamentary immunity (see paragraphs 51-52 above). The Court finds that these statements, which were made after the Court of Cassation’s decisions of 13 July and 8 November 2023, are not in themselves sufficient proof that there was an ulterior purpose underlying the applicant’s continued detention (see, mutatis mutandis, Selahattin Demirtaş (no. 4), cited above, § 316). That said, it observes that those statements were made before the Court of Cassation’s decision of 3 January 2024 declining to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgment on the applicant’s second individual application: a decision which led to the termination of the applicant’s parliamentary mandate on 30 January 2024 (see paragraphs 42, 47 and 161 above). In that regard, the Court also observes that those statements are consonant with the reasons put forward by the Court of Cassation when it declined to implement the judgments of the Constitutional Court (compare Kavala, cited above, § 229). Moreover, it cannot overlook the statements made by the President on 8 and 19 January 2024, which, in the applicant’s view, labelled him as a terrorist (see paragraph 51 above).

166. In assessing the relevance of the statements by the President of the Republic and his adviser for the purposes of Article 18, the Court attaches importance to the concerns raised by the Venice Commission and the Commissioner of Human Rights regarding the independence and impartiality of judiciary in Türkiye (see paragraphs 65-68 above; also compare Kavala (no. 2), cited above, § 273, with regard to the Court’s assessment of certain contextual circumstances indicating an environment of political and media pressure that was capable of affecting both the appearance and the reality of independence and impartiality on the part of the courts dealing with that case). It also regards the former and current Commissioners’ misgivings about the detention of human-rights defenders, including the applicant, as important. It reiterates that reports or statements by international observers, non‑governmental organisations or the media, or the decisions of other national or international courts are often taken into account, in particular, to shed light on the facts, or to corroborate findings made by the Court (see Merabishvili, cited above, § 317).

167. In that regard, in opinion on amendments to the Constitution, adopted at its 110th plenary session (CDL-AD(2017)005), the Venice Commission expressed the view that the proposed new composition of the Council of Judges and Prosecutors was “extremely problematic”. It observed that under the new constitutional system the President was not a neutral figure but belonged to a political group (see paragraph 68 above; also see Selahattin Demirtaş (no. 2), § 434, and Selahattin Demirtaş (no. 4), § 317, both cited above). In her report of 2020, the then Commissioner expressed concerns regarding the independence of the judiciary and its vulnerability to political influence, considering – with reference to the Court’s finding of an ulterior purpose in Selahattin Demirtaş (no. 2) and Kavala – that public statements by members of the executive and legislature criticising courts and commenting on ongoing cases could undermine judicial independence and influence judicial decision-making. She considered that the concerns about the authorities having the ulterior purpose of silencing human rights defenders had also applied to the other defendants in the Gezi trial, that is, the co-defendants of Mr Kavala (see paragraph 65 above). In her memorandum of 2024, the Commissioner reiterated her previous findings regarding the independence and impartiality of the judiciary in Türkiye and further underlined the damage caused to the rule of law by the failure to implement Constitutional Court judgments. In that regard, she pointed to the President’s statements regarding the applicant’s case, which, in her view, was exacerbated by the Court of Cassation’s stance (see paragraph 66 above).

168. The Court finds that the above-mentioned circumstances, taken as a whole, demonstrate that the applicant’s continued detention in the absence of recognition of his parliamentary immunity – which resulted from the Court of Cassation’s refusal to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgments – pursued the ulterior purpose of silencing him and stifling pluralism, and was liable to have a dissuasive effect on the work of human-rights defenders (see, mutatis mutandis, Kavala, cited above, § 232). At this point, the Court reiterates that the Convention was designed to maintain and promote the ideals and values of a democratic society governed by the rule of law (see Navalnyy, cited above, § 173). The ulterior purpose pursued in the present case is therefore of particular gravity, given the prominent role of human‑rights defenders in a pluralist democracy (see, mutatis mutandis, Kavala, cited above, § 231, and Kogan and Others v. Russia, no. 54003/20, § 77, 7 March 2023).
169. There has therefore been a violation of Article 18 of the Convention in conjunction with Article 5 of the Convention and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.
APPLICATION OF ARTICLEs 41 and 46 OF THE CONVENTION
Application of Article 41 of the Convention
170. Article 41 of the Convention provides:

“If the Court finds that there has been a violation of the Convention or the Protocols thereto, and if the internal law of the High Contracting Party concerned allows only partial reparation to be made, the Court shall, if necessary, afford just satisfaction to the injured party.”

171. The applicant claimed 50,000 euros (EUR) in respect of non-pecuniary damage. Without specifying an amount, he submitted that following the termination of his parliamentary mandate on 30 January 2024 (see paragraph 47 above), he had been deprived of the salary he had been receiving as an MP. He asked the Court to consider that aspect of the violation of his rights. The applicant did not make a specific claim in respect of pecuniary damage or costs and expenses.
172. The Government contested the applicant’s claim in respect of non-pecuniary damage, finding it excessive and incompatible with the Court’s case-law.

173. Ruling on an equitable basis, the Court awards the applicant EUR 32,500 in respect of non-pecuniary damage, plus any tax that may be chargeable. In the absence of any specific claim in respect of pecuniary damage or costs and expenses, it considers that it is not called upon to make any award to the applicant under those heads.
Application of Article 46 of the Convention

174. The applicant applied for his immediate release and the implementation of the Constitutional Court’s judgments in his favour, including its orders as to redress. The Court will examine the applicant’s request under Article 46 of the Convention, the relevant parts of which read as follows:
“1. The High Contracting Parties undertake to abide by the final judgment of the Court in any case to which they are parties.
2. The final judgment of the Court shall be transmitted to the Committee of Ministers, which shall supervise its execution.

175. The Court reiterates that its judgments are essentially declaratory in nature and that, in general, it is primarily for the State concerned to choose, subject to supervision by the Committee of Ministers, the means to be used in its domestic legal order in order to discharge its obligation under Article 46 of the Convention (see Guðmundur Andri Ástráðsson v. Iceland [GC], no. 26374/18, § 312, 1 December 2020). However, in certain special circumstances the Court has found it useful to indicate to a respondent State the type of measures that might be taken to put an end to the situation – often a systemic one – which has given rise to the finding of a violation. Sometimes, the nature of the violation does not leave any choice as to the measures to be taken (see Ilgar Mammadov v. Azerbaijan (infringement proceedings) [GC], no. 15172/13, § 153, 29 May 2019).

176. In the circumstances of the present case, the Court considers that the continuation of the applicant’s detention on account of his conviction and the resulting effects on his parliamentary mandate would entail a prolongation of the violation of his rights as well as a breach of the obligation on the respondent State to abide by the Court’s judgment in accordance with Article 46 § 1 of the Convention. It therefore finds that the respondent State must take all necessary measures to put an end to the applicant’s detention and secure his immediate release, and allow him to take up his seat in the Parliament and perform his parliamentary functions.

177. Furthermore, with regard to general measures, the Court emphasises that full compliance with the Constitutional Court’s judgments is essential to the rule of law (see paragraphs 122-123 above). It reiterates that the failure to implement that court’s judgments is likely to undermine the effectiveness of the individual application procedure, while compromising the constitutional order by depriving applicants of the effective application of their recognised rights (see Kavala (no. 2), cited above, § 314). It is therefore for the respondent State to take all appropriate general measures in order to provide that the judgments of the Constitutional Court are fully implemented and to prevent similar future violations.
FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT
Declares, unanimously, the application admissible;
Holds, by six votes to one, that there has been a violation of Article 5 § 1 of the Convention;
Holds, unanimously, that there has been a violation of Article 5 § 4 of the Convention;
Holds, by six votes to one, that there has been a violation of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention;
Holds, by six votes to one, that there has been a violation of Article 18 of the Convention in conjunction with Article 5 of the Convention and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention;

Holds, by six votes to one, that the respondent State is to take all necessary measures to put an end to the applicant’s detention and to secure his immediate release, and to allow him to take up his seat in the Parliament and perform his parliamentary functions, and that it is incumbent on the respondent State to take all appropriate general measures in order to provide for the full implementation of the judgments of the Constitutional Court and to prevent similar future violations;
Holds, by six votes to one,

that the respondent State is to pay the applicant, within three months from the date on which the judgment becomes final in accordance with Article 44 § 2 of the Convention, EUR 32,500 (thirty-two thousand five hundred euros) in respect of non-pecuniary damage, plus any tax that may be chargeable, to be converted into the currency of the respondent State at the rate applicable at the date of settlement;

that from the expiry of the above-mentioned three months until settlement simple interest shall be payable on the above amount at a rate equal to the marginal lending rate of the European Central Bank during the default period plus three percentage points;
Dismisses, unanimously, the remainder of the applicant’s claim for just satisfaction.
