PARTLY DISSENTING, PARTLY CONCURRING OPINION OF JUDGE YÜKSEL

I agree with the majority’s finding of a violation of Article 5 § 4 of the Convention. However, I am unable to share the majority’s view that there have been violations of Article 5 § 1 and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, and of Article 18 of the Convention taken in conjunction with those provisions.
AS REGARDS ARTICLE 5 § 1 OF THE CONVENTION AND ARTICLE 3 OF PROTOCOL No. 1 TO THE CONVENTION

1. In the present case, the applicant’s complaints under Article 5 concern whether he was entitled, under Articles 83 and 14 of the Constitution, to parliamentary immunity following his election as a member of parliament (MP) in the general elections of 14 May 2023. The interpretation of those provisions directly determines the “lawfulness” of the applicant’s continued detention following his election for the purposes of Article 5 § 1. The scope of the Court’s assessment of the applicant’s complaint under Article 5 § 1 thus covers the period from 14 May 2023, which pre-dates the Court of Cassation’s refusal to implement the Constitutional Court’s judgments delivered in the applicant’s individual applications (see paragraph 84 of the present judgment). Accordingly, the reasoning under Article 5 § 1 and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 goes beyond the issue of the non-implementation of the Constitutional Court’s judgments. In concluding that the applicant’s detention was unlawful, the majority endorse the Constitutional Court’s interpretation of Articles 83 and 14 of the Constitution and find that those provisions lacked the foreseeability required under the Convention (see paragraphs 92-93 of the present judgment). The decisive question in this case is whether Article 5 § 1 of the Convention requires the exception to be specified in legislation before it can be applied or whether judicial interpretation can suffice, and if the judiciary’s interpretation of this exception creates an issue of foreseeability. For the following reasons, I do not consider that Article 5 § 1 imposes such a requirement or that there has been a violation of it.

2. As regards the constitutional framework, Article 83 § 2 of the Constitution provides for two exceptions to the general rule of parliamentary immunity enjoyed by MPs. The exception relevant to the present case provides that an MP may not benefit from immunity in respect of a criminal investigation into the “situations referred to in Article 14 of the Constitution”, if the investigation was instituted before his or her election. Article 14 of the Constitution prohibits the abuse of fundamental rights and freedoms and provides, inter alia, that none of the fundamental rights in the Constitution may be exercised to undermine the unity of the nation or to extinguish the democratic and secular Republic founded on human rights. It is comparable in its function to Article 17 of the Convention.

3. In the domestic practice, it would appear to have been undisputed until 2021 that the offences falling under this exception were to be determined by way of judicial interpretation. That year, the Constitutional Court held in Ömer Gergerlioğlu that the text of Article 14 of the Constitution was framed in terms which did not lend themselves to interpretation by the judiciary in a foreseeable manner (see paragraph 103 of that judgment). It held that, in the absence of legislation identifying the offences covered by the “situations referred to in Article 14 of the Constitution”, that exception could not be applied in a coherent and foreseeable manner.

4. However, the Court of Cassation had already, in respect of the text of the two constitutional provisions, developed a body of case-law, pre-dating the Constitutional Court’s 2021 judgment, in which it had identified the offences capable of falling within the “situations referred to in Article 14 of the Constitution”. It had held that the legislature had not specified the offences falling within that exception, and that it therefore fell to the courts, in the exercise of their ordinary function of interpreting and applying the Constitution and the law, to do so. In this connection, the Court of Cassation had held that the exception covered the offences of disseminating propaganda in favour of a terrorist organisation, membership of an armed terrorist organisation, and attempting to overthrow the government by force and violence (see, for example, decision no. E. 2013/9110, K. 2013/12351 of 9 October 2013 of the Ninth Criminal Division – see also paragraphs 26-33 of the Constitutional Court’s judgment in Ömer Gergerlioğlu for a summary of the Court of Cassation’s case-law, which dates back to 2008, regarding offences that fall within and outside the exception).

5. It would admittedly be preferable for the legislature to specify by law the offences falling within the exception in Article 83 § 2 of the Constitution. However, the issue in the present case concerns the applicability of a constitutional provision as things stand. In this regard, Article 83 § 2 of the Constitution refers to “situations” foreseen under Article 14, not to a list of offences, and it thus does not presuppose a legislative catalogue of offences.

6. I would also note that in its two judgments concerning the applicant’s individual applications, the Constitutional Court did not specifically assess whether the offence of attempting to overthrow the government by force (under Article 312 of the Criminal Code) could fall within the situations referred to in Article 14, but relied on its general finding that the second exception to parliamentary immunity in Article 83 § 2 was inapplicable in the absence of legislation specifying the offences concerned. It could be said that the Constitutional Court’s interpretation has the effect of rendering Article 83 § 2 of the Constitution inoperative unless Parliament intervenes, although the wording of the relevant constitutional provisions contains no such prerequisite.
7. While the Constitutional Court’s interpretation is one possible reading of the Constitution, I do not consider that the Convention requires such an approach.

8. Against the background of this discrepancy between the two superior courts’ interpretation, the question before the Court is whether the interpretation followed in the applicant’s case met the standard of “lawfulness” under Article 5 § 1. According to the Court’s case-law, where deprivation of liberty is concerned it is essential that the conditions for it under domestic law be clearly defined and that the law itself be foreseeable in its application, so that it meets the standard of “lawfulness” set by the Convention, a standard which requires that all law be sufficiently precise to allow the person – if need be, with appropriate advice – to foresee, to a degree that is reasonable in the circumstances, the consequences which a given action may entail (see Medvedyev and Others v. France [GC], no. 3394/03, § 80, ECHR 2010, and Khlaifia and Others v. Italy [GC], no. 16483/12, § 92, 15 December 2016). However, the fact that a provision is open to more than one construction does not suffice to render it unforeseeable, the role of adjudication vested in the courts being precisely to dissipate such interpretational doubts as remain (see, mutatis mutandis, Sanchez v. France [GC], no. 45581/15, §§ 125-26, 15 May 2023). Moreover, the term “law” in the Convention comprises not only statute but also the case-law of the domestic courts, and a legal basis may accordingly be found in judicial as well as in legislative sources (see, in the context of Article 5 § 1, Baranowski v. Poland, no. 28358/95, §§ 50-58, ECHR 2000-III, where the Court’s objection was to detention having no basis in either legislation or case-law). The same applies to the notion of “prescribed by law”, in which context the Court has repeatedly found that the “law” in question must be understood to include both statutory law and judge-made “law” (see, among other authorities, Sanoma Uitgevers B.V. v. the Netherlands [GC], no. 38224/03, § 83, 14 September 2010; The Sunday Times v. the United Kingdom (no. 1), 26 April 1979, § 47, Series A no. 30; and Casado Coca v. Spain, 24 February 1994, § 43, Series A no. 285-A). In short, it can be said that the “law” is the provision in force as the competent courts have interpreted it.

9. It is difficult to see any case-law precluding exceptions to a general rule from being determined by way of judicial interpretation. As stated also in the judgment, what matters for the purposes of “lawfulness” is foreseeability. Having regard to the Court’s case-law, in my view, the Convention does not condition the applicability of an exception to parliamentary immunity of this kind on the legislature enumerating the offences covered by the Constitution, and judicial interpretation of that provision may suffice to satisfy the lawfulness requirement, provided that such interpretation is sufficiently foreseeable in view of the specific facts of a given case.

10. In this connection, it may be noted that on some occasions, the Court of Cassation’s interpretation may have been unforeseeable, in particular as concerns offences relating to freedom of expression. For instance, according to the Constitutional Court, one example was the Court of Cassation’s finding that Article 14 of the Constitution covered the offence under Article 7 § 2 of the Counter-Terrorism Act (as in the case of Ömer Gergerlioğlu). However, the fact that Article 14 was interpreted extensively in a different case concerning a different offence does not render the provision itself unforeseeable.

11. Moreover, at the time the Court of Cassation ruled on the applicant’s initial release request, the Constitutional Court had not yet specifically ruled on whether Article 312 of the Criminal Code fell within the exception provided under Article 83 of the Constitution. Furthermore, the applicant was convicted at first instance of the offence under Article 312 of the Criminal Code in April 2022 and has been detained continuously since then. It is difficult to see the basis for concluding that, when he stood for election in May 2023, the applicant was not in a position to know the Court of Cassation’s case-law according to which the relevant offence fell within the exception under Article 83 § 2.

12. Whatever difficulties the reference to Article 14 may present at its margins, what is relevant for the purposes of the Convention is whether the application of that interpretation to the applicant’s continued detention for the relevant offence can be regarded as unforeseeable. In my view, the application of that interpretation to the applicant’s continued detention cannot be regarded as either arbitrary or unforeseeable. The present case is thus different from previous precedents such as Aydın Sefa Akay v. Türkiye (no. 59/17, § 115, 23 April 2024) and Baş v. Turkey (no. 66448/17, §§ 189‑96, 3 March 2020), in which the Court found that the domestic courts’ interpretation ran counter to the provisions designed to protect the applicants and negated the safeguards those provisions afforded. Here, by contrast, Article 83 § 2 itself refers to situations covered by Article 14, and the discussion is as to whether reading Article 312 of the Criminal Code into that reference applies it to the very type of offence it appears designed to cover, rather than stretching it.

13. Lastly, since the majority’s finding under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 rests essentially on the same reasoning as that under Article 5 § 1, the considerations set out above apply equally to that complaint as well.
AS REGARDS ARTICLE 5 § 4 OF THE CONVENTION

14. That said, disagreeing with the Constitutional Court’s interpretation of the constitutional provision is one thing, but non-implementation of its decisions is another. It is beyond doubt that the execution of its judgments is an indivisible component of the right of individual application and that failure to comply with them amounts to a manifest and serious violation of that right. In addition, I share the Constitutional Court’s analysis that the non-execution of its judgments is likely not only to undermine individual and societal confidence in the rule of law, but also to compromise the constitutional order, by depriving applicants of the effective enjoyment of their recognised rights.

15. As the Court has recently emphasised, for another domestic court to call into question the powers conferred on a constitutional court to deliver final and binding judgments on individual applications runs counter to the fundamental principles of the rule of law (see Kavala v Türkiye (no. 2) [GC], no. 2170/24, § 132, 25 August 2026). Moreover, non-enforcement of the Constitutional Court’s judgments undermines not only the binding nature of those judgments, but also the ultimate purpose of the review provided for under Article 5 § 4, which is to obtain an order for release where the detention is found to be unlawful (see paragraphs 118 and 120 of the present judgment). A failure to enforce the Constitutional Court’s rulings is thus likely to undermine, more generally, the judicial protection of fundamental rights. For these reasons, I agree with the majority that there has been a violation of Article 5 § 4.
AS REGARDS ARTICLE 18 OF THE CONVENTION

16. With regard to the applicant’s complaint under Article 18 in conjunction with Article 5 of the Convention and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, I disagree with the majority’s view that there has been a violation of this provision. The majority consider that proof of an ulterior purpose can be established beyond reasonable doubt in the present case (see paragraph 158 of the judgment). Having regard to the burden-of-proof requirement in establishing that the measures complained of in the present case pursued an ulterior purpose, contrary to Article 18 of the Convention, I do not perceive sufficient grounds to conclude that there has been a violation of this provision. The Court must base its decision on “evidence in the legal sense”, in accordance with the criteria laid down by it in Merabishvili v. Georgia ([GC], no. 72508/13, §§ 309-17, 28 November 2017), and its own assessment of the specific relevant facts (see Khodorkovskiy v. Russia, no. 5829/04, § 259, 31 May 2011, and Ilgar Mammadov v. Azerbaijan, no. 15172/13, § 140, 22 May 2014).

17. In my view, the fact that there is a discrepancy between the two courts’ interpretation in the present case cannot be viewed as demonstrating that an ulterior motive was being pursued. Moreover, the Constitutional Court conducted a detailed assessment of the applicant’s complaints and found a violation of his rights protected under the Constitution and the Convention. In these circumstances, it is not possible to conclude that the entire judicial mechanism of Türkiye was acting in line with a political agenda when rejecting his request for release. Accordingly, I am also unable to agree with the majority’s findings under Article 46 of the Convention.
